New Zealand’s largest egg supplier is putting hundreds of thousands of free-range chickens into lockdown after the deadly bird flu virus was detected in the country for the first time.

Mainland Poultry, which supplies nearly 40% of the country’s eggs, has taken the precautionary step of isolating more than half a million free-range laying hens while officials work out the extent of the disease’s spread.

Contact the NZ Herald newsroom

While there have been zero cases of bird flu identified in commercial poultry flocks, and meat and eggs remain safe to eat, chief executive John McKay said the two detected in wild birds for the first time last week had prompted them to try to mitigate the risks.

McKay, who is also the chair of the Egg Producers Federation (EPF), told Ryan Bridge TODAY the nationwide agribusiness had just over 1.3 million hens, with around 550,000 of those farmed as free-range.

Free-range hens are usually given the freedom to spend much of their day outside and can interact with other wildlife, so McKay said Mainland Poultry staff had a “pretty busy weekend” closing off the pop holes in barns until more is known.

“The birds naturally come in in the evening. They come in to roost and have their final feed before they go to sleep,” McKay said.

“In the morning, [the pop holes] aren’t opened as per usual ... so the birds are temporarily housed inside those barns for their welfare.”

McKay said free-range eggs made up about 45% of New Zealand’s total egg market, so there was clear consumer demand.

Mainland Poultry would continue to maintain good on-farm biosecurity, even ramping up some measures, as McKay said it was crucial for protecting their hens and businesses.

“Obviously, we care deeply about our birds,” McKay said.

“Let’s better understand the risk, understand where it might have spread or where it hasn’t spread, and then based on better understanding that risk, we can then make good decisions about what we do with those birds going forward.”

New Zealand’s first known case of the H5N1 strain was recorded on Wednesday in a wild brown skua found on Lower Hutt’s Petone Beach, with a second detection in a native kāhu, or swamp harrier, in the Wairarapa announced Friday.

In an update yesterday, MPI’s chief veterinary officer Dr Mary van Andel said no new cases of bird flu had been found since, but they had received a surge in reports about dead or sick birds since the public notification and would be continuing to investigate each one.

Authorities hadn’t found any evidence of widespread transmission or mass mortality affecting wildlife either, she added.

“We have staff on the ground over the weekend carrying out checks in some areas of Wellington’s south coast and Wairarapa,” van Andel said.

“We continue to have a strong response from the public about unwell or dead birds they have seen, and we consider every notification and triage any suspected cases of avian influenza.”

Van Andel urged people not to touch or move the birds they encounter.

“If you see three or more sick or dead wild birds in a group, report it immediately to the exotic pest and disease hotline on 0800 80 99 66 from anywhere in New Zealand or online at report. mpi. govt. nz."

‘Simplistic’ colour-coded school reports get mixed reviews from principals

New Zealand Herald July 19, 2026

Principals fear that people will base judgments on tables rather than read full reports. Photo / 123rf

By John Gerritsen of RNZ, RNZ Morning Report

The publication of the first Education Review Office reports using colour-coded tables to depict schools’ performance has done little to allay principals’ fears.

The tables use four colours to show how schools are going in 14 areas, including attendance, reading and writing and teaching.

The colours show if schools are judged to be excelling (dark green), doing well (light green), working towards (orange) or improvement required (red).

Some principals worry the tables are too simplistic and will unfairly stigmatise schools in poor communities, where achievement and attendance is often lower than average.

The Education Review Office acknowledged the concern, and told RNZ it was particularly important people read the full reports of schools in poor communities and not base judgments just on the tables.

Westlake Girls’ High School was among the first schools to receive one of the new reports.

Its table was mostly dark-green squares, with some light green and one orange, meaning the school was “excelling” in most areas, “doing well” in others and “working towards” in just one area – attendance.

Principal Jane Stanley said it provided a better overall picture of the school’s performance than previous reports – but only if people read the full document.

“It’s certainly much more comprehensive than the previous ones were, and I think gives a really good picture of the school and what’s going well, and things that might need to be added to or improved.”

Stanley said many parents would likely only read as far as the table.

“It’s a really short summary of the work behind the full report.

“Unfortunately, people will probably go to that, and be drawn to that and not read behind.”

Beaconsfield School, near Timaru, also received one of the new reports. Its table was mostly light-green squares, plus some dark green and two orange – for attendance and school governance.

Principal Hamish Brown says the table said a lot, but it did not tell the full story.

“The boxes are okay,” he said. “They’ve indicated what they’ve found, but there’s two steps behind those boxes and we feel that anybody reading it is not going to go deeper into the report.”

For example, he said Beaconsfield received an orange rating for governance, because the school board had three new members, not because of any particular problem.

As for attendance, Brown said, with 120 pupils, a small number of children could have a big effect on the school’s percentages.

Brown said he knew other schools were apprehensive about the new reports.

“There is a bit of nervousness simply because it is very black and white, and sometimes communities, local people, papers, local media like to grab the short story without getting the full story.”

New Zealand Principals’ Federation president Jason Miles said the tables were confronting and could be misleading if people didn’t read the rest of the report.

“It is very easy for someone to look at those colour ratings, without reading the details behind it to get a certain impression of some schools,” he said.

He said the federation was worried that the attendance rating in particular was more a reflection of a school’s socio-economic status than how good the school was.

“A school that may have had 40% attendance and worked really hard to increase it to 60%, but will still be marked in the ‘working towards’ area, rather than be rated on the hard work and support that they’ve put in to raising that attendance.”

The Education Review Office understood the concern that some people may look only at the colour-coded snapshot.

“The snapshot is only one part of the report,” it said. “It is designed to help parents and whānau navigate the report, not replace the full report.”

The office said reading the full report was particularly important for schools serving communities with high levels of need.

“Where a school is making strong progress from a low base, or where teaching and leadership are effective, that will be recognised in the report,” it said.

“Each judgment is supported by narrative commentary explaining what the school is doing well, where improvement is needed and what actions will support better outcomes for learners.”

It said the purpose of the reports was to support school improvement, and the changes were aimed at making reports clearer, more accessible and easier for parents, whānau, schools and boards to use.

“We will continue to listen to feedback from schools, parents and whānau as the new reports are used, so that our reporting remains clear, useful and centred on learners.

“We acknowledge that it will take time for people to adjust to the new format.”

Pregnant surrogate explains what it’s like to grow someone else’s baby

New Zealand Herald July 19, 2026

Amy said carrying a baby for another couple has been a privilege, but also much harder than expected.

Amy is a midwife and a heavily pregnant surrogate from the Bay of Plenty. She is carrying a baby for a gay married couple she met online. This is her story, as told to journalist Janhavi Gosavi.

The first time I had dinner with the parents of my surrogate child, I knew they were the right people to have a baby for.

They had flown to my home from Otago to meet me after months of speaking over messages and phone calls.

We were all excited and a bit nervous.

I didn’t know if it was okay for me to drink alcohol with my meal, in case it made a bad first impression. They didn’t know if I would get spooked and pull out of becoming their surrogate.

Twenty months later, I am now in my third trimester, 34 weeks pregnant with their baby.

It’s been a privilege but it’s also turned out to be a lot harder than I expected.

When I was training to become a midwife, I learned about surrogacy and how it helped people make families.

It seemed like an amazing, wonderful thing to do but I was very young at the time and had not had my own children yet, so I parked it.

A few years ago, a friend floated the idea of me donating my eggs, which sent me down my path of eventually becoming a surrogate.

I remembered how much I loved being pregnant with my own children and wanted to go through it one last time before it was too late.

There is no other time in your life when your body changes so much.

Feeling a baby move inside you and grow from week to week – it felt weird to think I might never experience that again.

Email janhavi. gosavi@nzme. co. nz

In 2024, I created an account on a website called Love Makes Families, which connects surrogates and donors to parents.

I found myself drawn to a gay married couple who seemed open and genuine.

They wrote honestly in their profile about why they wanted a baby and made it clear how loved their future child would be.

The process of getting to know them felt a lot like online dating.

The dads and I had long conversations about our expectations, what pregnancy-related costs they would pay for, and what kind of contact we would keep post-delivery.

Being a midwife, I wanted to discuss every possible scenario, including whether they would want to terminate the pregnancy if the fetus had a fatal condition.

A scenario I did not consider was me being bedridden for three weeks because of hyperemesis, a condition that causes extreme nausea and vomiting.

It had made my other pregnancies difficult, but this pregnancy is shaping up to be the hardest nine months of my life.

In my first 20 weeks of being pregnant, if I was not at work, I was in bed, feeling guilty that I might be a bad parent because all I could do was put food into the air fryer for my children.

When I would go to work, I would cry on the way there because the last thing I wanted to do was to be upright and mobile.

I’m still sick now and have found myself doing the unexpected: counting down the days until I can birth this baby.

I don’t want to wish the pregnancy away and I’m so excited for the couple to become parents, but I’m also excited to feel better soon.

My kids’ reactions to my surrogacy have been surprisingly mature.

At first, they didn’t want me to have the baby because they worried they would be sad about not being able to keep it.

My 8-year-old daughter changed her mind after she snuck into a Skype call I was having with the dads and told me she thought they would make good parents.

Adults, on the other hand, have struggled more at wrapping their heads around my decision.

Some people tell me I’m “amazing”, which makes me feel awkward because I’m bad at taking compliments.

Others go, “Woah, why would you do that?”

People want to know if I knew the parents already (I did not), if I used my own egg (I did), and a few love to share stories about how they almost did it themselves before backing out.

One lady at the supermarket asked if I thought it would be hard to give away my baby, which I thought was quite an intense conversation for the supermarket.

Most of all, people want to know how I could stand to “give a baby away”.

From the beginning, this hasn’t felt like my baby.

I do love it and I’m protective of it, but it’s different to when I carried my own children.

It truly does feel like I’ve got someone else’s baby growing in me – it’s mine for now but it’s not mine forever.

In seven weeks, I will be flying to a birthing centre to push a baby out for the last time in my life.

After the delivery, I will stay with the baby near the couple’s home for 12 days until I can sign over legal guardianship to them.

Under current law, I am considered the baby’s legal parent at birth.

The dads will eventually have to adopt their own child, even though one of them is the biological father, which is a process that could take up to a year.

The Improving Arrangements for Surrogacy Bill is going through its second reading in Parliament and, if it is turned into law, it will remove the need for this kind of adoption.

My plan is to stay present in this child’s life as an aunty figure, who will be kept updated on major milestones and will visit every so often.

I did not know my dad growing up, so having an open adoption is extremely important to me.

If this child ever has questions about where they came from, I want them to know they can call me up any time.

Across our in-person visits, I’ve seen how great the couple are with my kids.

I know that love is going to multiply tenfold with their own baby, and it’s been a privilege being part of making that happen.

Amy’s last name has been omitted to maintain her privacy.

Janhavi Gosavi is a Wellington-based journalist for the New Zealand Herald who covers news in the capital.

Search and rescue teams have searched the shorelines and island of Rotorua's Blue and Green lakes for Jeremy Robertson after the death of his mother in Pahīatua.

Police will conduct one last search for a Pāhiatua man they believe killed his own mother before fleeing town.

Jeremy Robertson is thought to have died shortly after leaving the Wairarapa town and arriving in Rotorua in October last year.

He is the sole person of interest in the investigation into the death of his mother, Karen Gilbert-Palmer in Pāhiatua.

Robertson, in his 50s, is believed to have taken a car from his mother’s property and driven about 350km to Rotorua, where the vehicle was found abandoned at the Blue and Green Lakes lookout on Tarawera Rd.

Since the car arrived at the carpark, there has been no activity on his bank accounts or mobile phone, Detective Sergeant Richard How said today.

Given this, police believe the most likely scenario is that he died shortly after arriving in the Green and Blue Lakes area.

On Wednesday, about 20 police Search and Rescue staff, alongside volunteers, will conduct a final planned search in the surrounding areas of the carpark of the lookout, where the vehicle was found.

“Police remain committed to locating Jeremy if at all possible, to provide the closure that Karen’s loved ones deserve,” How said.

Search efforts will include a drone search phase. The drone will be used to search around the lake and nearby islands.

“Police expect this search to be a single day operation, but will have a significant presence in the area throughout the day,” How said.

“We are urging the public to contact us with any information that could assist our investigation.

“We’d like to hear from anyone who has previously located any medication packets, or any red or blue clothing in the area surrounding the Lakes, and nearby tracks.”

Sport chiefs monitor slimming drugs as bodybuilding use surges

New Zealand Herald July 19, 2026

Wada, the World Anti-Doping Agency, notes an "alarming run" of weight-loss drugs among athletes. Photo / 123rf

Weight-loss drugs like Wegovy have been hailed as game-changers for patients with type 2 diabetes, but have now started to make their way into the competitive bodybuilding space.

Global hype around the GLP-1 receptor agonists has surged in recent years, both for clinical and cosmetic purposes, with their rising availability and visibility on the world stage sparking active dialogue among various sporting federations.

The World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada) has added Semaglutide and Tirzepatide, the active ingredients in Ozempic and Wegovy, and Mounjaro, respectively, to its monitoring programme – noting an “alarming run” in the non-diabetic community, including among athletes.

Wada said this allows it to track patterns of their use in sports in and out of competition, but as neither of these ingredients are presently prohibited, there are no existing consequences for the athlete if found.

Wada is reportedly considering banning slimming drugs outright before the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics – with a decision to be based on health risks, whether they give users an unfair advantage and whether they violate the spirit of sport.

Eric Helms, the co-director of the AUT Sport Research Institute New Zealand (Sprinz) and a natural bodybuilder, said these medications are already being used in the “enhanced” or untested competitive bodybuilding space.

This is particularly the case in the US, where they can be accessed through wellness clinics, as opposed to traditional GPs.

Helms said the drugs are also growing in popularity among recreational non-competitive bodybuilders who are simply trying to maintain lower body fat.

But he said their use is typically banned in drug-tested, “natural” federations without a therapeutic-use exemption.

Insulin manipulators currently feature on the International Fitness and Bodybuilding Federation Pro League New Zealand (NZIFBB) prohibited substances list when used solely for weight-loss purposes.

The NZIFBB said it conducts natural drug-tested competitions and tests athletes for a range of prohibited substances at all its events, including anabolic steroids and diuretics.

It said, to date, athletes tested at its natural competitions have consistently returned negative results.

Helms said athletes in untested divisions tend to be more willing to experiment with performance- and image-enhancing drugs.

He said these bodybuilders are sometimes taking high-dose anabolic steroids, androgens and other substances that enhance the ability to carry muscle mass and get leaner over decades.

Helms said natural competitors tend to be more risk-averse.

He said the value GLP-1 receptor agonists offer in bodybuilding is less about a shortcut to weight loss, because these athletes are typically already well-educated and meticulous about nutrition.

But he said they can make contest preparation easier, by suppressing a lot of the food noise that comes with getting as lean as possible in the cutting phase, and some people take them post-competition to have more agency over rebounded weight gain.

Helms said the argument for and against the use of these drugs is complex, with various philosophical and moral, legal and safety reasons for why certain substances should be banned – but for him, it ultimately comes down to the spirit of the sport, and equitable fair play.

He said natural bodybuilding revolves around bringing whatever cards you were dealt to the table and using discipline, knowledge, training and experience to get as far as you can.

Helms said the idea of making that process easier, to the point where it’s not a challenge, is antithetical to many and to the concept of natural bodybuilding.

He said there are also access barriers, because of cost and availability, and permitting the drugs could force athletes who might not want to take them to do so, to feel they are on a level playing field.

Helms said GLP-1 receptor agonists are incredibly helpful for the intended clinical population when used in the right way – but there should be a notable distinction between people dieting as part of a competitive physique sport and people using these medications as an adjunct for health.

Claudia O’Neill is an Auckland-based Multimedia Journalist for Newstalk ZB with an interest in science, health and geopolitics. She holds a Bachelor of Science degree from the University of Auckland and a Postgraduate Diploma in Journalism (Distinction) from Massey University. She joined NZME in 2023.

US says another troop killed as Israel warns Tehran’s attacks coming close

The Guardian Sun, 19 Jul 2026 20:16:44 GMT

US military says service member was killed in Iraq during ‘controlled detonation’ as it launches more airstrikes at Iran

The US military announced another death of a service member as it launched more airstrikes at Iran on Sunday in response to the killing of American troops , and Iran fired missiles toward Jordan that risked widening the conflict into neighboring Israel.

The US military said the service member was killed in Iraq on Saturday during the “controlled detonation” of a downed Iranian drone.

Earlier, the military said its strikes targeted Iran’s paramilitary Revolutionary Guard to retaliate for Friday’s killing of troops in Jordan. One service member was missing after that attack, and the military’s new statement said “unidentified remains” were found on Sunday and were being examined. Since the war began, 17 US service members have been killed.

Step by step, the US and Iran have returned closer to all-out war as last month’s interim deal meant to permanently end the fighting has crumbled and shipping traffic in the strait of Hormuz has largely stalled. Both sides have targeted civilian infrastructure relied on by millions of people.

The renewed exchanges of fire, now in their second week, have seen the US target bridges, water desalination plants and electrical facilities in Iran. Tehran has hit US-allied countries throughout the Middle East.

Kuwait, Jordan and Bahrain again activated air defenses for incoming Iranian drones and missiles. Israel warned that missiles launched toward neighboring Jordan could cause fire to spill over into Israeli territory for the first time in weeks.

The US military’s Central Command said it hit “Iranian military coastal surveillance and air defense facilities, maritime capabilities and missile and drone storage sites”. It said the attack was designed to degrade Iran’s ability to control the strait and “swiftly punish Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps forces”, a power base in Iran’s theocracy that controls its ballistic missile arsenal.

Footage released by the US military appeared to show strikes carried out by fighter jets and by Tomahawk cruise missiles launched from the sea. One target site appeared to be in a valley of a mountainous region. The Guard often has missile bases and other military equipment tucked into mountain ranges.

Iran’s atomic energy agency said US strikes targeted the construction site of a planned nuclear power plant in the southwest, state television reported.

Satellite images from Planet Labs PBC of the Darkhovin nuclear plant site showed earth clearing but little construction as of 9 July. Iran did not previously announce it as being targeted.

The International Atomic Energy Agency said the site, in the “very early stages of construction”, contained no nuclear material when the UN watchdog last visited.

Iranian authorities on Sunday said at least 50 people have been killed and 517 wounded in the latest US strikes. Iran has provided no overall information on its materiel losses.

Far from the region, the war’s effects on the prices of fuel and other goods have hit some of the world’s most vulnerable areas hard.

Glory eludes hometown hero Tommy Fleetwood in his dream made reality

The Guardian Sun, 19 Jul 2026 19:55:33 GMT

Southport local said the ovation he received on the 18th was ‘incredibly special’ after his title chances fizzle out

Two o’clock on a sunny Sunday afternoon, five hours or so to go in the 154th Open Championship, and here comes Tommy Fleetwood up the 1st fairway, five shots off the lead. A delay in one of the groups up ahead meant that Fleetwood has had to stand and wait 15 minutes at the tee box, which is maybe why, when he finally got up to play his opening shot, he pulled it left into the rough stuff behind a fairway bunker. It was the first time he’d missed that shot all week.

From there, Fleetwood had caught his second shot a little thinner than he wanted. He shrugged as he followed its flight, twisted his lips into a grimace as he watched the ball drop and stop about 20 metres short of where it needed to be. “Head up, kid!” someone cried out. “Head up!”

On Saturday night, Fleetwood said he had been imagining this Sunday at the Open just about as long as he can remember. “I’ve done it most days since I was seven years old, and it still hasn’t stopped,” he said. “That’s what life’s about, right? You dream about the biggest things possible and then you try and make it a reality.”

Now here it was at last, real as it gets. Sunday at Royal Birkdale, a clear blue sky over his head, parched brown grass beneath his feet, a shot at the Open Championship in front.

And his home crowd all around, every step of the way. “Walking up to every green, it’s like the most amazing ovation that you can imagine,” Fleetwood said. These aren’t strangers on the other side of the ropes, they’re friends, and friends of friends. They’re people he was at school with, used to play football with, people who worked with his dad, or used to get their hair cut by his mum, people who worked with him sweeping leaves at Southport & Ainsdale, who shared a drink with him in the clubhouse at Formby Hall.

“I still try to stay in my bubble,” Fleetwood said. “It just happens that there’s like thousands of people in my bubble with me that are willing me on.” However many times he pictured the moment in his head, he can’t ever have been standing over this putt in front of him on the 1st, 73ft from the front of the green to a pin set tucked into the very back corner.

But here it is. And now the ball is rolling and all of a sudden people are starting to shout out and the ball’s closing in and now even the marshals who are supposed to be controlling the crowd have turned around to watch and as it drops into the cup everyone’s up and screaming and leaping and Fleetwood is pumping his fists and the roar they made in that moment must have carried clean over the beach and out across the Irish Sea.

Four shots back became three shots back when Fleetwood drove the green and chipped his second shot on for a tap-in birdie at the 5th. By the time he made an 8ft putt for birdie on the 8th he was only two shots behind. He was eight under now, and in that moment everyone there on the course, and watching on TV, listening on the radio, felt that maybe, just maybe, he really was going to do it. Like Fleetwood said himself: “Sometimes dreams do come true, we watch it all the time.”

And sometimes they don’t.

At the 9th Fleetwood overhit his approach and it skittered off the green over the back up into the lee of the grandstand. Everyone watching winced. It got worse. His next shot was his ugliest yet. It blew 30ft past the hole, and this time, as hard as everyone around hoped for him, he wasn’t able to hole it. It was his first bogey, and it seemed to break the spell. He dropped a second shot at the 10th, when he blew his tee shot wide right, and a third at the 11th, where he took three putts. That meant he had dropped three shots in as many holes.

He would say later that the par-five 14th was the one that finished him. He was greenside with a chip for birdie, but it burned the hole and passed 3ft by.

“My dream might come true, it might not,” Fleetwood had said last week, “but you’ll never find out if yours will unless you chase it.” By the time he got to the 18th, just before six o’clock, the gallery had made peace with the idea that it wasn’t going to happen for him this year. Maybe he had too. He scored a birdie on 17, was an inch off holing his approach on 18. That left him seven under, three shots off the winning score, tied for fourth.

“There’s disappointment that I didn’t win when I was in a good position, but the atmosphere walking down 18, that was beyond anything I ever dreamed,” Fleetwood said. “As a kid, when you’re dreaming of having putts to win the Open, that’s one thing, but I could never imagine something like that ovation on 18. That was incredibly special.”

Ryan Fox crowned Open champion as heavyweights wilt under pressure

The Guardian Sun, 19 Jul 2026 18:57:40 GMT

USA’s Cameron Young falls short by a single shot

Rory McIlroy hints at DeChambeau joining Irish Open

What a way to enhance a family dynasty. Ryan Fox, son of a New Zealand rugby legend and grandson of one of the country’s cricket captains, is the Open champion. Three generations, three sports, one Claret Jug. Fox displayed the fortitude of Grant, his old man, to snatch victory from Cameron Young on such a dramatic Open Championship Sunday.

Fox took to the 18th tee level with Young at nine under par. The American had finished more than two hours earlier, his total looking ever-more promising as others took it in turn to wilt under the heat of Royal Birkdale. Fox laughed in the face of adversity. He crashed a drive 330 yards down the fairway, flicked an iron to 11ft and holed out for a birdie three. This will trigger quite the party, including in his homeland. This Open needed something to switch the conversation from Bryson DeChambeau and a rules breach. In Fox, the tournament found a bold and deserving champion.

For Young, there will be pain. A par at the last would have earned him 10 under par and, as it was to transpire, a playoff. He found the bunker from the 18th tee. A six-iron, intended to reach the front of the green, rebounded from the top of the trap and into thick grass. Young, who is becoming a major nearly man, scrambled superbly for a bogey five. It was not enough, alas.

On a week dominated by sunburn and grass burn, some believed it was fate that Sam Burns would triumph. Instead, the 54-hole leader wobbled after reaching 11 under inside two holes. He regressed to minus eight at the turn, where he was to stay. It was Fox who was to deal best with golf’s version of scorched-earth syndrome.

At one point, it looked as if matters were conspiring against Fox. His tee shot to the perilous par-three 15th hit the bank of a bunker, from where it flew back to a position where the 39-year-old had no scope to even hit his ball forward. Fox escaped with a four. He had an opportunity to reach double digits under par on the penultimate hole yet missed. In the clubhouse, a pensive Young was edging ever closer to extra holes. He was denied that by a Fox attack.

Kim Si-woo had taken the lead when holing from off the green at the 6th. He remained in the equation until a poor closing stretch. Kim shared sixth with Casey Jarvis and Lucas Herbert.

Tommy Fleetwood, the hometown hero, could not end his major wait at Birkdale. Still, the moment of Sunday belonged to him. He kissed his hand, waved and touched his heart in front of adoring galleries after holing out for a 72nd-hole birdie. If there really are golfing gods, he will win an Open. His finish this time was a tie for fourth. Things had started so promisingly on Sunday for Fleetwood, who triggered roars that reverberated around the course with a birdie from 73ft on the 1st.

Scottie Scheffler should really have become the first man to win back-to-back Opens since Padraig Harrington here in 2008. The taking of 32 putts in round two fatally harmed the world No 1’s cause. Scheffler flew from the traps on Sunday, throwing darts towards flags and playing the first five holes in three under. He had slipped to six under on the 15th but roared back again; birdies at the 16th and 17th left him one from the lead while playing the last. Scheffler carved his tee shot right, missed the green and took three from there. A finish beside Fleetwood at minus seven was a real tale of missed opportunity. “I guess it just wasn’t my week,” Scheffler said. His consistency of results remains quite incredible.

Bob MacIntyre’s latest tantrum, this time slamming his driver into the ground, received a code of conduct warning from tournament officials. “I’m going to do it for the rest of my career,” the Scot said. “I try and toe the line, but when you feel you’re playing a golf course that you can hit it pretty much anywhere and there’s no real punishment and then you do hit one slightly off line and you get the biggest punishment you can possibly get, it’s just a sore one. I’m going to react aggressively at times. Part of my DNA.” Perhaps it shouldn’t be. Professional golfers set examples.

DeChambeau was hovering on the leaderboard before a disastrous triple-bogey seven on the 11th. The record books will show a tie for 14th as his best major finish of 2026. The R&A quietly breathed a sigh of relief that he did not close only two from the lead, that being the penalty for his errant footwork on the 5th during Friday’s round.

The leaving of a bunker shot by the 18th green in sand rather summed up Rory McIlroy’s Open. The Masters champion signed off with a 71 for a one-under total. McIlroy will now take a holiday before returning to competitive action in the PGA Tour’s playoffs. He was asked rather mischievously whether he would welcome DeChambeau at the Irish Open this year, as has been rumoured as a possibility. The event takes place at Donald Trump’s Doonbeg resort. “I think that would be great for the tournament, absolutely,” McIlroy said. “Having someone like Bryson at the Irish Open, it would be great for the tournament.”

McIlroy’s scathing sentiment towards DeChambeau had been the theme of Saturday at the Open. Day four proved just as eye-catching. Inside the ropes, this time. Fox has just sampled a life-changing moment.

Burnham to say UK must be honest about its challenges as he prepares to become PM

The Guardian Sun, 19 Jul 2026 18:32:36 GMT

Labour leader will visit king to accept role on Monday and will start making cabinet appointments that afternoon

Andy Burnham will say Britain must be honest about the challenges it faces when he becomes its sixth prime minister in a decade on Monday, as he prepares to introduce measures to ease the cost of living and allow more North Sea fossil fuel drilling.

The Labour leader is expected to start making appointments in the afternoon after going to Buckingham Palace to accept the role of prime minister from the king.

Many cabinet ministers and even some of Burnham’s allies were still in the dark on Sunday about whether they would be offered positions in his top team, although there is a widespread belief Shabana Mahmood will be made chancellor and Ed Miliband foreign secretary.

The chief whip, Jonathan Reynolds, is also regarded as nailed on as business secretary of a department incorporating the current science and technology department. The former cabinet minister Lou Haigh is expected to be the leading Cabinet Office minister.

The former deputy prime minister Angela Rayner, is said to be lined up for the job of health secretary, but sources said she would take some persuading that it was the right fit for her when her main interests are in devolution, regional inequality, local government and the cost of living.

Before a policy blitz next week, Burnham’s first Downing Street address will seek to strike an optimistic but also realistic note about the problems facing Britain that must be confronted.

He is expected to say the country faces a moment for “reflection and resolution”, having previously said he was willing to spend political capital on fixing major problems such as social care that will require extra funding.

On measures to help people’s finances, he is likely to take steps to bring down energy billsand may target bus fares. Sources said he is also preparing to open the door to more oil and gas drilling in the North Sea in existing areas, despite a backlash from environmental campaigners and some MPs. Burnham will also say he is “acutely conscious” of being the sixth person to walk up Downing Street in 10 years and argue that political stability is needed – in an implicit rejection of calls for an election when Labour potentially has another three years in power.

He will say Britain must be honest about the challenges it faces while demonstrating that it can again be recognised around the world for effective government.

The Labour leader will go on to set out his domestic priorities, saying he will deliver tangible improvements in people’s lives and give people “more breathing room” when it comes to the cost of living.

Burnham has not so far made any major policy commitments beyond saying he would stick broadly to Labour’s manifesto commitment of not raising VAT, national insurance or income tax, and scrapping the digital ID card programme.

His allies have signalled he would be prepared to speed up the pace of current drilling in the North Sea, including potentially adding to existing fields, without approving major new fields in line with the manifesto.

Donald Trump appeared to believe Burnham was preparing a significant policy shift, congratulating him on Saturday night for agreeing to go “all the way” in opening up new fields. He wrote on Truth Social: “The People of Aberdeen, in Scotland, are dancing in the streets because the new Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, has stated that he will be opening up, all the way, the invaluable North Sea Oil!”

Labour’s deputy leader, Lucy Powell, had earlier said Burnham would take a more pragmatic approach and that it was a “change of emphasis” rather than a change of policy.

Burnham’s greater openness on North Sea oil and gas was one factor in Miliband falling from favour as frontrunner to be chancellor, given his opposition to more drilling as energy secretary.

He is being tipped instead for foreign secretary and could take a more pro-Gaza position and greater steps towards setting the UK on a pathway towards restoring foreign aid to 0.7% of national income from its current level of 0.2%. The idea was immediately seized on by Reform UK. Its leader, Nigel Farage, said: “Andy Burnham plans to spend an extra £10bn of your money on foreign aid. I will always put British people first.”

Burnham’s team also declined to be drawn on his plans for Thames Water after the Sunday Times reported he was expected to push the London and south-east England utility company into a special form of administration in an intervention that could mean the state has to pay some of its running costs until a buyer is found.

Powell spoke on Sunday about Burnham’s plans for increased public ownership, saying the economy had been “overly privatised” and the “utilities and essentials of life don’t work in the interest of ordinary people.”

She said bills were “going up and up because they are run in the interests of private interest, not for the consumers or for taxpayers”.

The Conservatives have accused Burnham of planning to put up taxes in order to fund areas that will need more money, from social care to defence. When asked about a wealth tax, the new Labour leader said he did not want to create divisions, but that in the future an option “might be having to ask for a little more”.

Kemi Badenoch criticised Burnham on Sunday for not setting out his plans before Monday and not having done in-depth media interviews before taking office, describing his comments so far as “airy-fairy stuff”.

The Conservative leader told the BBC she thought Burnham was “a people pleaser” rather than someone who would make tough decisions.

Fossil fuels, utilities and housing: what we know about Andy Burnham’s plans

The Guardian Sun, 19 Jul 2026 17:00:32 GMT

Incoming prime minister has set out distinctly leftwing vision while also promising to be pro-business

As an incoming prime minister promising huge change, one of the strongest criticisms Andy Burnham has faced so far is that he has failed to provide the details of what he plans to do.

The new Labour leader, who will be made prime minister on Monday, has thus far set out a distinctly leftwing vision, while also pledging to be “pro-business”.

But in the absence of leadership contest hustings or opportunities for the media to subject him to probing interviews, there are gaps in what is known about his plans for government.

Here is what we do know so far.

Burnham has pledged to take more public control of key utilities such as water, a move that appears likely to begin with Britain’s largest water company, Thames Water.

He is also understood to be considering radical plans that could cut household energy bills by £130 a year and make running a heat pump cheaper than a gas boiler. The proposals would change the way household gas is charged and remove some policy levies from bills, at a cost of £3.2bn a year to the taxpayer.

Thames Water, which serves 16 million customers and has been on the brink of collapse for several years, will meanwhile be put into a special form of administration until a buyer is found, according to the Sunday Times.

Expect action, too, on transport policy. Burnham has said he would be informed by the transformation of the Greater Manchester bus network during his time as mayor, which included taking the system back under public control from private operators.

Speculation is rife that Burnham will announce fresh plans for drilling in the North Sea.

The Labour leader’s team has not publicly confirmed the details of its North Sea policies and whether they would involve new exploration licences or “tiebacks”, where offshore oil and gas fields are connected to already approved production facilities via pipelines.

In its 2024 manifesto, Labour pledged to honour existing exploration licences but not issue new ones.

The Guardian understands that the tieback arrangements would allow new drilling to take place without technically breaching the manifesto commitment, although any new activity is likely to anger some backbenchers and climate campaigners.

Even before his Makerfield byelection victory made him an MP again, Burnham’s allies had briefed that he would be supporting Shabana Mahmood’s controversial changes to the immigration system.

On Monday, and back in the House of Commons, he supported the government’s asylum changes, voting for legislation that has divided Labour MPs over plans to tighten the immigration system and reshape the appeals process.

While he has avoided laying out specific policies in the area in key speeches, he has said recently that net migration needs to fall further and spoken of how voters in Makerfield “raised their concerns about immigration”.

Burnham is expected to scrap Keir Starmer’s plans for digital ID cards in a “reset of priorities”, redirecting resources earmarked for the scheme towards tackling the cost of living.

The proposals were outlined at the weekend in an attempt to distance the incoming prime minister from unpopular choices made by his predecessor. A petition opposing the introduction of digital ID cards when it was announced last year attracted about 3m signatures.

Keir Starmer first announced the digital ID scheme last September, as part of a strategy to combat illegal working. It was to be introduced by 2029.

Burnham’s team have asked officials to draw up plans to abolish the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT) as part of a wider Whitehall shake-up.

However, while the plans have triggered an angry backlash from MPs, Whitehall officials and others, a new cabinet on Monday is expected to include a minister for artificial intelligence for the first time.

The proposals in relation to the DSIT would hand over much of science and technology policy to a more powerful business department, to be led by the chief whip, Jonathan Reynolds.

The prime-minister-in-waiting highlighted fixing social care as a priority, vowing last week to “grasp the nettle” of adult social care reform.

Burnham first tried to change the social care system when he was Labour’s health secretary in 2009. At the time, he proposed a levy on estates to pay for universal social care, but he has since talked about replacing inheritance tax with a progressive “care levy” to fund a national care service.

Speaking to the Guardian on the campaign trail last month, he said: “I personally would look at all of the kind of implications of that in relation to inheritance tax and care charges and everything. I wouldn’t flinch from it.”

Burnham has said he wants the government led by him to “oversee the biggest council house building programme since the postwar period”.

The challenge is a major one, the scale of which is seemingly not lost on Burnham, who linked the loss of almost 1.5m council homes since the 1980s to the number of families on social housing waiting lists nationwide rising to a similar level.

In a hint of other plans, he has also said that high costs are having a “ruinous impact” on the government finances amid record levels of taxpayer support allocated to housing, much of which flows to private landlords.

The Guardian view on perceptions of superpowers: the world isn’t Chinamaxxing, it’s America-avoidant

The Guardian Sun, 19 Jul 2026 16:30:31 GMT

Startling new research shows that in many countries – including old US allies – the public prefers Beijing to Washington

Earlier this year, a spate of western TikTok and Instagram creators announced that they were at “a very Chinese time in my life” – drinking hot water and wearing slippers around their homes. The Chinamaxxing phenomenon primarily reflected the constant need of influencers for novel content. But social media trends also reflect a growing fascination with China, as the economic historian Adam Tooze has noted.

While it broods over China’s economic, military and technical advance, the Trump administration is accelerating Beijing’s diplomatic progress, as striking new polling by the Pew Research Center shows. For the first time, China and Xi Jinping are seen more favourably than the US and its president in most of the 36 major countries surveyed – including Canada, Mexico and Australia. Only in six countries did people rate the US more highly. While Beijing has seen significant improvements in some places, the slump in Washington’s standing is more dramatic. Across 20 countries, the median percentage with a favourable view of China rose from 32% to 46% between 2023 and this year; for the US, it fell from 58% to 36%. Views of China were much more positive in Latin America, Africa and parts of south and south-east Asia than in wealthier European and east Asian countries.

On Thursday, Mr Trump accused China of interfering with the 2020 election – casting doubt on polls ahead of midterms that are forecast to hit Republicans hard. Never mind the lack of evidence; he offered Argentinians a $20bn economic incentive to vote in line with his preference last October. In nearly every country surveyed, more people thought the US interfered in other countries than thought China did so. Mr Trump’s demands to take over Greenland, the abduction of Venezuela’s then leader Nicolás Maduro and the illegal war on Iran have all left their mark. Even the World Cup, which should have been an easy US soft power win, has been tarred by his exclusion and bullying.

Grave concerns about Beijing remain. Though it has dialled back displays of aggressive “wolf-warrior” diplomacy, it is forceful in its dealings. But it may benefit from lower expectations, and it looks predictable beside Trump-created turmoil. Famously, Beijing has just one ally: North Korea. Washington has more than 50 – but seems to accord them less respect than adversaries. Beijing detained two Canadian citizens for more than 1,000 days in retaliation for Ottawa’s arrest of the Huawei executive Meng Wanzhou due to a US warrant. But Mr Trump announced that Canada will be the 51st state.

China is increasingly investing in overseas influence operations, including working with or amplifying local social media content creators. Content may range from paid-for Xinjiang travelogues intended to erase concerns about the persecution of Uyghurs, to softer material about food or technology.

The Pew findings may further convince it of Washington’s hegemonic decline. China is keen to encourage the belief that it is leaping into a shiny new future of cyberpunk cities, while the west struggles with a declining standard of living – not least because it is useful in the face of domestic disillusionment.

But public perceptions of other countries are often complex and volatile. US standing rebounded after dropping sharply over the Iraq war; China’s favourability ratings fell during the pandemic, reflecting its handling of the outbreak. The lasting lesson for both superpowers should surely be that presentation shapes opinion, but others will judge them on their actions – and respond accordingly.

The Guardian view on pubs: football gave them a boost – now they need another

The Guardian Sun, 19 Jul 2026 16:25:31 GMT

Communal spaces where people can share big moments are a vital part of our shared life

“People can’t get enough of football fever,” a pub landlord, Sam Hale, told the Guardian last week. The World Cup provided the UK’s struggling hospitality industry with a much-needed boost, with pubs benefiting from extended opening hours and one estimate suggesting that an extra 5.5m pints were sold in the group stages alone. The tournament lifted customers’ spirits too – even if it ended in disappointment for England and Scotland fans – as millions of people relished the communal spectacle.

These sociable few weeks could not have come at a better time for pubs, which are closing at a rate of two a day, with about 2,000 gone since 2020. This reflects a long-term trend away from going out, combined with pressures from rising costs including energy bills, business rates, wages and national insurance contributions. The hope in the sector, and among its advocates, is that the temporary uplift of the past few weeks will focus minds on the importance of venues, including pubs, in promoting social cohesion and “watercooler moments”.

The wider industry is campaigning for a halving of VAT on hospitality from 20% to 10%, and more than 288,000 people have signed a petition. Given the likely cost to the Treasury of at least £10bn, this proposal is unlikely to be taken up. A thinktank, Tax Policy Associates, has pointed out that multinational businesses, including McDonald’s, would be the biggest beneficiaries. But with a recent survey finding that almost a quarter of pubs and restaurants are losing money, ministers should be looking for ways to help.

This is not just a matter of owners’ finances. Spaces where people can meet and talk to each other, and share special occasions, are an important part of our collective life. The American sociologist Ray Oldenburg coined a name for them, “third places”, and pubs are not the only ones that fit the bill. His point was the value of the public realm more widely – parks, libraries, youth clubs. And it is important to recognise that pubs’ overall impact includes harms linked to alcohol. But sales of no- and low-alcohol beer are booming and, particularly in rural areas, pubs are vital facilities at a time where loneliness is also a serious public health issue.

The shrinking number of entry-level jobs in sectors including hospitality is another concern. In his interim report for the government on young people and work, Alan Milburn argued that this is one factor behind the rising number of 16- to 24-year-olds who are neither in work nor education.

It is easy to be nostalgic about pubs, as it is about many things that are associated with the past. They are not the be-all and end-all of thriving neighbourhoods. One reason why people are staying in more is that there is more to watch on television than there used to be. It is good if people enjoy being in their homes.

But there is real value in making an effort to be around others, having face-to-face conversations rather than tapping out messages. Recent research has pointed to social isolation among young adults as a growing problem. Experts differ as to explanations, but the pandemic, home working and social media have all been suggested. A worthwhile legacy of this World Cup would be a strengthened recognition of the value of shared, in-person experiences after the fever has died down.

The group of investors pursuing a rescue bid for Thames Water have said they are willing to discuss greater public control but are also preparing for a potential multi-billion pound legal battle amid reports that Andy Burnham could temporarily nationalise the company.

London & Valley Water (L&VW), a consortium of 100 institutional investors that hold £17bn of the company’s £21bn debt, has said it is open to government involvement with Thames Water, but indicated that this does not include public ownership in the struggling company.

Mike McTighe, the corporate troubleshooter who is leading the governance overhaul and building the new board proposed for Thames, Britain’s biggest water company, said the consortium wanted to work constructively with Burnham when he takes over as prime minister.

“We are keen to meet new ministers as soon as possible to discuss how we can work together in the best interests of customers, including by enhancing public control of the company’s operations,” he said. “We will work with Andy Burnham, his government and local authority leaders to rebuild confidence in Thames Water and the wider sector.”

The comments by McTighe, who is likely to take over as Thames Water’s chair if the consortium is able to get its £10bn rescue deal approved by the government, follow reports that Burnham is planning to transfer the company into a special administration regime (SAR), a form of temporary public ownership, after he takes over as prime minister.

Burnham said last month that there should be “greater public control” of Thames Water and told the Guardian this could mean nationalisation.

The SAR proposal would transfer the costs of running the company to the taxpayer, with Thames Water’s creditors claiming the bill could come to £2bn.

“If it is going to cost the taxpayer £2bn to keep the company afloat then the taxpayer needs to receive something in return; that means control, so that we can fix the company and secure the water supply for thousands of families and businesses,” a Burnham ally told The Sunday Times.

L&VW, which includes fund managers such as Apollo Global Management, Elliott Management, Farallon Capital Management and Silver Point Capital, has also moved to strengthen its legal position in order to be prepared if Thames is nationalised.

The consortium has hired top litigation and disputes firm Pallas Partners to work alongside Akin Gump, the law firm advising the consortium on the terms of their restructuring proposals.

“Creditors are assessing all potential routes that the situation regarding Thames Water may play out,” said one person close to the consortium. “They want, and need, to be ready. There is no legal action being taken at this point. This is purely a precautionary measure.”

Earlier this month, Thames Water’s creditors were said to be still willing to pursue their bid for the debt-laden company, even if Burnham were to bring it into temporary nationalisation.

“The consortium is trying to pursue a solvent restructuring,” said the person. “This would avoid a taxpayer funded administration process and help creditors recover as much as possible. It can bid alongside any others, but that prolongs everything.”

The future of Thames, which serves 16 million customers in London and the Thames valley and is buckling under interest payments on debt it has run up since privatisation, will be one of the most pressing issues in Burnham’s in-tray when he enters Downing Street.

“We remain ready and willing to recapitalise Thames Water, return it to investment grade, and begin the long process of turning it around,” said McTighe. “We urgently need government engagement to begin that process.”

McTighe is the chairman of Openreach, BT Group’s infrastructure arm, and previously chaired the Daily Telegraph’s publisher.

The lenders have been trying to take ownership and bring it out of administration after a failed attempt to sell the utility to the US investment group KKR last year.

However, the creditors’ plans were thrown into doubt last month when Emma Reynolds, the environment secretary, wrote to the regulator, Ofwat, voicing concerns about the terms of the deal.

Vingegaard crashes out of Tour de France after ‘inhuman’ 2am doping control

The Guardian Sun, 19 Jul 2026 16:15:06 GMT

Dane was woken by doping control at 2am on day of stage

Remco Evenepoel outsprints Pogacar to claim victory

Jonas Vingegaard crashed out of the Tour de France on the first Alpine stage on Sunday, only hours after being woken up in the early hours to undergo doping controls. He will have collarbone surgery in the next few days.

The double Tour winner, who also won the Giro d’Italia this year, climbed gingerly into a race ambulance, his right arm in a sling, after falling as the main peloton exited a roundabout in Bonneville.

Vingegaard and Tadej Pogacar were subjected to unexpected nocturnal doping controls, outside the normal window of 6am to 11pm, before stage 15, as the race headed to Plateau de Solaison in the Savoyard Alps. Vingegaard was tested at 2am by the International Testing Agency (ITA), while Pogacar’s unexpected knock on the door came at 5am.

Pogacar described Vingegaard’s 2am wake-up call as “inhuman” and suggested that it “ruined” his longstanding rival’s sleep and could have been a factor in his crash. Before the stage start on Sunday, Vingegaard said: “I was sleeping very well. It’s good that they test, but when it’s affecting performance and your sleep, I don’t think it’s so good.”

Pogacar said the disturbance could “be a small percentage in why he crashed because he probably didn’t sleep good”, adding: “I know how it feels. They woke me up at five in the morning also, but at least I got my deep sleep. It’s better than if they come at two.”

Pogacar’s own performance seemed unaffected by the nocturnal disturbance. Once again he led the way up the final climb, this time with his UAE Emirates XRG teammate Isaac del Toro and Remco Evenepoel in tow, moving to the front of the race on the steep final climb, just as Vingegaard, cradling his right arm, gingerly climbed the steps to the Tour’s mobile hospital.

But for once Pogacar, the four-time winner, did not have the upper hand and was unable to come past Evenepoel, as the Belgian led home the sprint for the stage victory. Behind the trio, Paul Seixas and Florian Lipowitz – Evenepoel’s Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe teammate – gave chase but both lost almost a minute in the overall standings.

In a statement the ITA said: “The ITA is conscious that night-time testing may be disruptive to riders’ rest and recovery. Due consideration has therefore been given to minimise as much as possible the impact testing activities have on riders.

“However, the ITA, on behalf of the UCI [the governing body], has the responsibility to ensure the effectiveness of the cycling anti‑doping programme and the integrity of cycling races.”

The statement added that “effective testing must, in limited and justified circumstances, be capable to occur outside standard daytime hours. All testing activities conducted at the Tour are subject to the safeguards established under the world anti-doping code, the UCI anti-doping rules and French law, with due consideration for riders’ welfare, equity and fundamental rights.”

While nocturnal tests are highly unusual, the UCI’s rules state that tests outside the normal hours of 6am to 11pm may be allowed if there is a “serious and specific suspicion that the rider may be engaged in doping”.

Other teams confirmed that during the Tour they have also undergone tests as early as five in the morning. Pogacar said that recently the pattern of controls he had experienced had been “strange”, adding: “They’re doing different testing than usual. For example, I was counting how many controls I had at home since the first of January.

“When I was at home, I was already waking up every day at six to check the doorbell because I had so many visits. I didn’t want to go for dinner or the supermarket even, because they were coming at random hours.

“If this is necessary to still prove that we are riding clean, then I totally accept it and I commit to this, but it’s a bit shit when you sleep four hours in one day.

“If Jonas was tested at two in the morning, he slept less than four hours, it ruined his deep sleep and then completely ruined the night. But it is what it is, and if this is what we have to do, we do it.”

Evenepoel, meanwhile, who has now risen to second in the overall standings behind Pogacar, was typically outspoken. “To be honest, I would send my team tonight to wake them [anti-doping officials] at three in the night, to let them feel how it is, and to take blood,” the double Olympic champion said.

“It’s inhuman and this is something we actually should not accept as athletes, because everybody knows sleep is the only recovery that we have in the night. And if that gets disturbed, it makes it even harder. I hope it doesn’t happen any more in the future because it’s quite disrespectful.”

‘What has the BBC ever done for me?’ Romesh Ranganathan reboots corporation’s 1985 licence fee plea

The Guardian Sun, 19 Jul 2026 16:02:20 GMT

John Cleese’s 1985 advert for the BBC in which he asks a pub full of stars “What has the BBC ever given us?” is one of the most famous examples of the corporation making the case to the public for the value of paying the licence fee.

In the advert, Cleese is complaining to the bartender that he has just bought his TV licence. “Fifty-eight quid for the privilege of sitting in your own home, watching your own television set. It’s diabolical. I mean, what’s the BBC ever given us for 58 quid?” he says, before being put right by a string of punters, ranging from David Attenborough and John Humphrys to Terry Wogan and David Jason.

Now, over 40 years later, as the corporation cranks up its campaign for the charter that allows it to operate to be renewed, it has rebooted the advert with a new musical version fronted by Romesh Ranganathan and directed by Dougal Wilson, the man behind Paddington in Peru and the John Lewis Christmas ad campaigns.

The comedian stars as a disgruntled licence fee payer grumbling in EastEnders’ Queen Vic pub to a host of household names including Chris Martin, Claudia Winkleman, David Jason and Greg James.

The comedian then has a whistle-stop song and dance tour of the BBC’s shows and services, featuring about 90 famous faces, from Alan Carr to Cate Blanchett, from Hey Duggee to Clive Myrie.

The BBC faces what its director general, Matt Brittin, described recently as “a moment of real jeopardy” due to a decline in licence fee payments and the rise of rivals such as YouTube, TikTok and the streamers. The number of people paying the BBC’s licence fee fell faster than expected in the last year, with half a million more households opting out of the payment.

To illustrate what could be lost, near the end of the advert Ranganathan is propelled to the backstage of Strictly Come Dancing to meet Louis Theroux, who says: “You know, none of this has to exist,” as he puts his hand on the lever of a giant on/off switch marked BBC, “if we don’t want it to”.

The film is being premiered on TV during the World Cup final and was launched on social platforms on Sunday morning. It has had some positive reaction from viewers, but a lukewarm response from some quarters, with the Telegraph complaining that the selection of BBC offerings presented were “notably middlebrow” and the Times complaining that – as is “sorely emblematic of so much TV content these days on the BBC, but also elsewhere” – it was a rehash of an old idea.

There have been a number of BBC promotional films over the years aimed at encapsulating its public service offering in a way that informs, educates and entertains.

They include star-studded versions of the Beach Boys’ God Only Knows and Lou Reed’s Perfect Day. But Cleese’s ad (itself based on Monty Python’s Life of Brian scene What Have the Romans Ever Done For Us?) was highlighted recently by Chris Packham as “genius” while promoting an open letter in defence of the corporation.

Ranganathan defended the rationale behind the new version, saying: “I strongly, strongly believe that the BBC should exist and, look, don’t get me wrong, I don’t think it’s without its flaws.”

“There have definitely been times and issues where I wished it could have dealt with things differently – but I feel incredibly passionate about the fact that we should have it and it adds so much to our lives. And I’m really proud of it.”

“I really do feel strongly that we should have a BBC and I think that there is nothing else that does what the BBC does.”

He said when he was asked to front the film, “I was very surprised that they’d chosen me and very honoured, but I thought it was a no-brainer, really.”

Growing up, it was the BBC’s Goodness Gracious Me that made him believe he could have a performing career, he said: “I didn’t think people that looked like me could do comedy. I was doing standup as a little kid and then you watch something like Goodness Gracious Me and you think, yeah, I could do that.”

The advert acknowledges that the BBC has done a lot for Ranganathan himself, with Myrie pointing out he fronts The Weakest Link, Sara Cox reminding him he hosts a Radio 2 show and Chris McCausland highlighting his “hip-hop podcast on Sounds”.

Nesrine Malik’s incisive piece (In Israel’s prisons, torture and death have become a norm that it barely tries to hide, 13 July) lays bare the fact that all the illegal detentions, deaths, torture and sexual abuse in Israeli prisons are not aberrations from a legal system, but deeply embedded in the practices and intentions of the state. She mentions the psychological dimension to deliberately eroding the capacity of Palestinian civil society to exert any kind of autonomy.

As mental health practitioners, working alongside our Palestinian co-professionals, we have long recorded the ways in which practices of degradation, humiliation and debilitation constitute attacks on minds and relationships as well as bodies. They are designed to undermine the fabric of family, social and community life, and to destroy those systems of connectivity upon which all citizens, especially children, are dependent if they are to flourish. The carceral system is part of a set of state interventions which not only detain, murder, maim and mutilate Palestinian bodies, but also conduct an unrelenting assault on their growth, dignity, personhood and identity.

Malik is right to highlight the extent to which western governments and most mainstream media act as if it is the “extremist fringes” rather than the state itself that should be criticised or sanctioned. Gwyn DanielUK and International Palestine Mental Health Networks

I’ve seen first-hand how to divert children away from lives of crime

The Guardian Sun, 19 Jul 2026 15:41:15 GMT

In the 1980s, I was director of the Northampton juvenile liaison bureau, which became a model nationwide, writes Jim Crook

I completely agree with Kirsty Brimelow that the age of criminal responsibility should be raised from the age of 10 to 14 (Jailing children does not make us safer – we need to get rid of this Dickensian delusion, 11 July). Also, that many more children could be diverted away from the criminal justice system. In the 1980s, I was director of the Northampton juvenile liaison bureau, a multi-disciplinary team that was successful in diverting more than 80% of the children between the ages of 10 to 17 who were offending away from the criminal justice system by employing informal methods of control, support and care, including restorative justice.

It gained a national reputation and became a model for the creation of youth-offending teams. Research revealed no increase in youth offending or repeat offences as a result of this policy. Due to the reduction in the number of juvenile court sittings and fewer children being processed through the criminal justice system, it saved in today’s money nearly £2m per year in Northampton alone and avoided children acquiring criminal convictions and criminal records. Research also found that the biggest impact on preventing further offending by the majority of children was being caught, spending a night in police cells, and the consequences of having to face parents. Jim CrookStillington, North Yorkshire

‘He’s a war criminal’: Mamdani exploring whether he can arrest Netanyahu if he visits New York

The Guardian Sun, 19 Jul 2026 15:38:11 GMT

NYC mayor says in Times interview that’s he’s in ‘active conversation’ with city’s law department about the matter

New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani has said he was reviewing whether his administration could arrest Benjamin Netanyahu if as expected the Israeli prime minister visits the city for the UN general assembly in September.

Mamdani’s comments on Saturday’s episode of the New York Times’s the Interview podcast echoed ones he had made to the publication as he successfully ran for mayor last fall.

“I believe that prime minister Netanyahu belongs in The Hague,” Mamdani said, referring to the Dutch city that is home to the international criminal court, which issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu in November 2024 over alleged war crimes in Gaza. “He’s a war criminal who has been charged by the international criminal court, and what you will find is that is an opinion that is held by many, purely because of what his actions have wrought over these past many years.”

Mamdani said it was unclear to him whether he has the legal authority to order the New York police department (NYPD), which he oversees, to detain a foreign leader like Netanyahu. But he said he was in “an active conversation” with the city’s law department about the matter.

“Whatever the law allows me to do in New York City, that’s what we will do,” Mamdani added. “But we won’t be writing our own laws to that end.”

The warrant which the ICC issued for the arrest of Netanyahu and other Israeli leaders accused them of war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, including “starvation as a method of warfare, and … murder, persecution, and other inhumane acts”.

During his mayoral campaign, Mamdani characterized Israel’s military actions in Gaza as a genocide and Netanyahu as a war criminal, telling the New York Times in September that he would order NYPD to arrest Netanyahu in the event he ever set foot there. He also condemned the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel as a “horrific war crime”.

The Times report back then cited legal experts who judged that having Netanyahu arrested “would be a practical impossibility” for Mamdani – and could bring him into direct conflict with the US’s federal government.

The US is not a party to the ICC and does not recognize its authority. And in February 2025, early in his presidency, Donald Trump ordered economic sanctions against the court, maintaining that it lacked jurisdiction over the US or Israel.

Trumps’s US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, then recently vowed to “dismantle” the court, accusing it of “waging a war against our country, not with bullets or missiles” but with “the force of so-called international law”.

Netanyahu, who faces a tough re-election campaign in October, brushed off Mamdani’s arrest threats in a recent radio appearance, saying he was not concerned.

Though Mamdani denies the accusation, Netanyahu also alleged Mamdani supports Hamas.

“He’s with the terror actors,” Netanyahu told New York’s WABC. “And I think the problem is that he doesn’t recognize and he doesn’t care that those who hate the Jews and Israel ultimately hate America.”

Israel’s ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, accused Mamdani – New York’s first Muslim mayor – of failing to confront rising antisemitism in his city. Mamdani has countered such accusations by noting that he has increased funding for an office to combat hate crimes.

“Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu will come to New York, address the United Nations General Assembly with pride, and stand before the world to state Israel’s truth and its unwavering right to defend its citizens,” Danon said.

Trump’s ambassador to the UN, Mike Waltz, also dismissed Mamdani’s threat as “pure political theater”, saying the US is not a member of the ICC.

World leaders from United Nations member-states are expected to travel to New York in September for the body’s annual session. Netanyahu has often participated in this event in previous years.

“We’re not talking about a personal assessment of Benjamin Netanyahu,” Mamdani told the Times’ podcast. “We’re talking about the international criminal court and the fact that they have a warrant out for this prime minister’s arrest, and I think it’s important to talk about the weight that that has as a charge and that also, as the mayor of New York City, I’ll be following the laws of New York City.”

Mamdani’s comments on Saturday came as his stance on Israel is becoming less fringe within the Democratic party.

Close to half of US House Democrats on Wednesday voted to strip $3.3bn in military aid to Israel. It was not enough to pass the measure. But it signified a buckling of unconditional support for Israel, a shift that is also reflected in public opinion polling.

Asked by the Times about the political weight he places on Israel and support for it by the US, Mamdani said ongoing war in Gaza was motivating voters throughout the country, including when his endorsed candidates swept House races in New York in June.

“It is hard to find a more bankrupt policy approach than what our country has done to Gaza and to Palestine,” he said.
