‘There was absolutely no chance of being a kid’: new exhibition explores how war shapes children’s lives

The Guardian Sun, 19 Jul 2026 15:00:31 GMT

Childhood in War examines what life looks like when play, education and family life is disrupted by hostilities

When John Hajdu was three, his parents gave him a teddy bear small enough to fit into his hands: 86 years later, it is the only surviving object from his childhood.

The bear, which the 89-year-old simply calls “teddy”, stayed with him as his father was taken to a labour camp, his mother sent to a concentration camp, and he hid in a non-Jewish neighbour’s cupboard before being forced into the Budapest ghetto.

From 31 July, teddy will go on public display for the first time as part of Childhood in War, a new exhibition at the Imperial War Museum, London, examining how conflict shapes children’s lives.

Displayed in a recreated second world war bedroom, the bear sits among toys, books and personal possessions that ask visitors to consider what childhood looks like when play, education and family life are disrupted by war.

The exhibition combines hundreds of objects with immersive environments, including a full-size railway carriage, a wartime classroom and a cold war living room and kitchen, alongside testimonies from children living through conflicts in places including Ukraine, Sudan and Afghanistan.

For Hajdu, teddy represents a childhood interrupted. Before the war, his life was typical of a well-to-do, middle-class Jewish family. By 1944, after years of antisemitic persecution in Hungary, his father had been sent to a labour camp and Hajdu and his mother had been forced into a designated yellow-star house.

“We could only take with us what we could carry, and that meant just a few pieces of clothing and teddy,” he says. “There was absolutely no chance of being a kid. I had no other toys or books. We were only allowed out in the afternoon wearing the yellow star. I couldn’t meet other children. We weren’t allowed in parks, cinemas or swimming pools or cafes. I was completely isolated.”

The exhibition explores exactly those everyday losses. A reconstructed classroom shows how war disrupts children’s education through objects from conflicts including the second world war, Northern Ireland, Afghanistan and the former Yugoslavia.

There are comics warning children about landmines and unexploded ordnance. Visitors can also climb into an evacuee train carriage containing letters sent home and Kindertransport objects, including a red knitted jumper given to Jochewet Heidenstein by her parents before she and her sisters fled Berlin for Britain.

In October 1944, Hajdu’s mother was arrested and taken to Mauthausen concentration camp in Austria. Believing she would never return, Hajdu’s aunt rushed him into the cupboard of a non-Jewish neighbour.

“I had teddy in my pocket,” he says. “I was in complete darkness and had to keep completely quiet. It seemed like a very long time, which was an incredibly frightening experience for a seven-year-old … By that time I was able to comprehend what happened without fully understanding the enormity of the situation.”

He later moved with his aunt into the Budapest ghetto, sharing a flat with more than 20 strangers. “There were no children. We survived on horse meat and bread. Dead bodies lay piled up on the streets, having died of cold, starvation or disease. I was always hungry. Again, I had teddy in my pocket.”

The ghetto was liberated by Soviet troops in January 1945, just before retreating German forces planned to destroy it. Miraculously, Hajdu was reunited with both his parents. His mother survived Mauthausen after US troops liberated the camp, but returned with broken ribs, smashed teeth and lasting psychological scars. “I was convinced I’d never see my parents again,” he says.

A decade later, after the Soviet suppression of the Hungarian uprising, Hajdu and his mother walked 40km (25 miles) and crossed an icy river under cover of darkness to reach Austria. They arrived in Britain in 1957 on a Red Cross train, with teddy travelling with them.

Throughout the exhibition, stories such as Hajdu’s sit alongside contemporary accounts from children living through war today. Visitors can explore a 360-degree virtual tour of an underground school in Ukraine created by one of its pupils, read poems written by Ukrainian children for Unicef’s Poems for Peace project, and see drawings by children in Sudan that were later submitted as evidence of alleged war crimes to the international criminal court.

A poem by a 15-year-old Afghan girl describes the moment the Taliban returned to power in Kabul in August 2021: “I witnessed how that day darkened not only Kabul’s sky, but also the dreams and hopes of so many.”

The exhibition also examines how childhood can become politicised, with material from the Hitler Youth and Soviet Komsomol movements.

“We wanted to talk about the impact of war on children’s lives,” says curator Fran Singleton. “With more conflicts in the news at the moment, it felt like the right time to create an exhibition that offers families a space to come together and discuss these important topics.”

For Hajdu, allowing teddy to leave his home for the first time has been surprisingly difficult.

“Teddy did, and still does, mean so much to me. It was my only connection to a family life I barely remembered when I was three,” he says. “I find it difficult to look at the desk where he normally sits.”

Now a grandfather of four, Hajdu spends much of his time speaking in schools about surviving the Holocaust. As the number of survivors dwindles, he hopes younger generations will continue telling these stories.

“I tell them, ‘When you go home, talk to your grandparents and parents. Find out whether they’ve gone through traumas, whether it’s in Asia or Africa.’

“My small story is an example that you can survive. Unfortunately, people are suffering all over the world. We are getting older, and fewer and fewer Holocaust survivors are here to tell these stories. It’s absolutely vital that the younger generation takes on what we’re doing.”

Rise in overseas surrogates ‘increases risk of stateless babies’

The Guardian Sun, 19 Jul 2026 15:00:29 GMT

Calls grow for global regulation as rising numbers of westerners use surrogates in countries with different laws

Why Mexico is at the heart of ethical debate over global surrogacy

The rise in the use of surrogates abroad is leaving more babies at risk of becoming stateless, experts have said, amid growing calls for urgent global regulation of the practice.

The warning follows the suspension of a 15-year effort by The Hague Conference on Private International Law (HCCH) to establish a global surrogacy convention, which was paused due to divisions among member states.

With more older women, gay couples and people affected by infertility seeking to become parents, increasing numbers of babies are being born to surrogates around the world. Surrogates normally carry pregnancies from a donor egg or the egg of someone who wishes to become a parent.

Laws differ from country to country, with some such as Italy banning the practice outright, while others, including some US states, allow commercial surrogacy. The UK only allows “altruistic” surrogacy, where surrogates cannot be paid more than their expenses from carrying the pregnancy.

UK surrogacy agencies argue that an outdated legal framework at home is pushing couples to seek surrogates abroad, where regulations to protect surrogates from exploitation can be less robust or do not exist at all. Anti-surrogacy campaigners say the practice is fundamentally abusive in all cases and are pushing for a global ban.

Prof Michael Hellner, who chaired the HCCH working group, said hugely differing opinions on the ethics of surrogacy between the member states involved meant the project to create a global framework on legal parentage in surrogacy cases had proved impossible.

“I invested 10 years of my life into this project. But if there’s no political will, there’s absolutely no point in us spending more of people’s time and money,” he said. “The lack of coordination between states on this issue leads to problems for the children, and the risk of statelessness is increasing.”

Hellner said the patchwork of cross-border surrogacy arrangements put babies at risk of “limping parentage” – where a child has different legal parents in different countries – and statelessness.

Experts said statelessness could happen in cases where a country does not automatically grant nationality to a child born there, and where surrogacy is not legally recognised in either the country of birth or the child’s final destination.

Hellner said the project had proved difficult when some countries were “violently opposed to anything that could be seen as legitimising surrogacy, which they think is a violation of human rights and dignity”.

There is no data on the number of births by surrogacy globally, but they have increased rapidly in the UK over the past decade, doubling since 2015 to more than 981 in 2025.

Most of these children were born abroad, mostly in the US, Ukraine, Nigeria, Georgia, Colombia and Mexico. British people using surrogates abroad to have babies are forced to apply to the UK family courts for a parental order to become the legal parents of their child and, in some cases, also need to apply for British citizenship for the child.

Maud de Boer-Buquicchio, the president of the Geneva-based nonprofit Child Identity Protection and a former UN special rapporteur on the sale and sexual exploitation of children, said the HCCH was a missed opportunity to have explicit international standards on the recognition of legal parentage in surrogacy, which can be a requirement for establishing nationality.

“There are lots of situations where these children are just left in a limbo and that affects their legal status, which is something that is crucial to having an identity,” she said. “The differences in legislation between different countries is still a big, big puzzle.”

The subject of international surrogacy came to prominence this week when Jens Spahn, a former German health minister and ally of the chancellor, Friedrich Merz, was forced to resign his position in his party after revealing he and his husband used a surrogate mother to become parents – a practice he had criticised in the past and his party is vehemently opposed to.

Member states involved in the HCCH included the US, UK, Australia and Canada, where surrogacy is permitted in some form, as well as France, Germany, Italy and Spain, which have heavily restricted or banned surrogacy domestically.

Bhaskar Mishra, a child protection specialist at Unicef, said the UN agency was pushing for better guidelines to protect the rights of children in international surrogacy.

“If the government doesn’t issue a passport in either the country where the baby is born, or where it is going home to, then there are chances the baby will become stateless,” he said. “That’s a serious risk in cases of international surrogacy agreements, and numbers are growing, and growing very fast.”

In 2025 a senior UK judge issued a warning about risky surrogacy arrangements abroad after a couple faced a four-year legal battle to bring two children born via surrogacy to Ukrainian women in Cyprus back to the UK, during which time they were essentially stateless.

The then president of the family division, Andrew McFarlane, said the case should act as a warning that courts may refuse to grant a parental order in cases where a child was born via commercial surrogacy abroad and this may leave the child “permanently stateless and legally parentless”.

Last year, Denmark was forced to change its laws to allow legal parentage recognition in foreign surrogacy arrangements, after the European court of human rights ruled that preventing this violated children’s rights.

The UN’s special rapporteur on violence against women and girls, Reem Alsalem, has called for surrogacy to be abolished globally, calling it a “system of violence, exploitation and abuse against women”.

Alsalem said women and girls who were “impoverished, destitute and affected by crisis and conflict” were more likely to be exploited by surrogacy arrangements, and commissioning individuals usually came from “western wealthier states”.

“The vulnerability to exploitation and abuse through surrogacy would not be possible if it were not for the existence of demand by commissioning individuals, who are usually from western wealthier states, a dynamic that reinforces colonial and discriminatory practices,” she said.

“There is a push to normalise and legalise surrogacy worldwide, given that it is lucrative and there are many strong and well-financed powerful lobbies behind it.”

Marie-Josèphe Devillers, who runs the International Coalition for the Abolition of Surrogate Motherhood (CIAMS), said she worked with surrogates who regretted their decision, and said they felt “cheated, lied to and exploited”.

One woman was a victim of human trafficking from Latin America to France, and another, from the US, said her child was sold to people other than those she had believed to be the intended parents. Devillers said she had also looked at cases where women had experienced health complications during pregnancy or birth, including some deaths.

Michael Johnson-Ellis, the founder of My Surrogacy Journey, which facilitates surrogacy in the UK, US and Mexico, said as long as it was done ethically and with proper regulation, international surrogacy worked well.

“People should be allowed to make a choice on where and how they do surrogacy, providing it’s safe and there’s no risk of people being exploited or coerced,” he said. “The wait time is about two years for a UK surrogate, and for some people who have been on a lengthy journey with infertility, that time might be something they don’t have.”

He said his agency only recommended the US and Mexico for parents seeking surrogates abroad, and was vocal in advising people on where to avoid. “We see the horror stories through the high courts of people being stuck in places like Cyprus or Georgia or Ukraine, or some of these emerging destinations that clearly are exploitative and dangerous,” he said.

Rachel Westbury runs Nappy Endings, a UK-based surrogacy agency, and has been a surrogate four times since 2011. She said desperate parents were increasingly looking abroad for surrogates but the number of suitable countries was narrowing.

“People need to stop thinking that it’s just celebrities doing it and glamourising it. It’s not just for millionaires. We have people who remortgage their home to do it,” she said. “It’s a privilege to be a surrogate. If more people knew the magic of surrogacy, when it’s done right, more surrogates would come forward.”

Why Mexico is at the heart of ethical debate over global surrogacy

The Guardian Sun, 19 Jul 2026 15:00:29 GMT

Many say lack of regulation allows people to exploit women’s bodies, but others argue it offers financial freedom, and a child to those with no other option

Rise in overseas surrogates ‘increases risk of stateless babies’

Diogo Amaro met his future husband, Loup, in Paris and from the first date, he made one thing clear: he wanted to have children.

“Right off the bat, I was like: ‘If I’m going to be in a relationship with somebody, I really want to build a family,’” he said. “‘That’s important to me, so please tell me if you want to walk.’”

But Loup didn’t walk – in fact, the couple moved to New York together a few months later and after five years they were married in a ceremony back in Paris.

Surrogacy is banned in France, as well as in Germany, Italy, Spain, Sweden and Switzerland. In the UK, surrogacy can only happen on altruistic terms; paying a surrogate is illegal, but intended parents are permitted to cover expenses.

The rules in Amaro’s native Brazil were restrictive and complicated, and the United States was prohibitively expensive.

Instead, like an increasing number of Europeans from countries with surrogacy bans, Amaro and his husband chose Mexico, where the practice is widespread and largely unregulated. Only two states have banned it and another three have regulations governing the practice.

Because it is not regulated at a federal level, there are no reliable numbers for how many surrogate pregnancies take place in Mexico. This lack of regulation can also become deeply problematic for those involved, according to advocates.

“The current model – characterised by uneven or nonexistent regulation – does not offer sufficient guarantees for pregnant people,” said Verónica Esparza, from Mexican reproductive rights group GIRE. “Surrogacy agreements are frequently carried out in contexts of cultural, economic and social inequality.”

Keith López Nares is a professor at the University of the Valley of Mexico and co-author of a 2024 study on the practice of surrogacy in Tabasco, one of the only states where the practice is regulated.

The study found that surrogacy was “a patriarchal practice of reproductive exploitation that affects the most vulnerable women living in poverty, leading them to rent their wombs as a survival strategy.

“This situation of economic vulnerability is exploited by the international and national markets as an extractive practice justified by the argument that women ‘freely’ decide to sign the surrogacy contract.”

According to Lopez Nares, some poor women in Tabasco were coerced by their husbands into undergoing surrogacy multiple times. In some cases, husbands took over the surrogacy process outside the clinic or agency structure.

“It became a personal business: instead of being under the strict orders of a clinic’s instructions, they would be directly able to organise, manage and control the resources obtained from the exploitation of their wives’ bodies.”

As far as the business involving foreigners, Lopez said it was a “form of neo-colonisation of women’s bodies”.

“You take children from Mexico, and then you don’t know what happens to them,” she said. “I mean, nobody, nobody demands any accountability regarding the whereabouts and wellbeing of these children.”

GIRE has also documented numerous irregularities in Mexico, including contracts with vague or ambiguous clauses that left women vulnerable, as well as “problems for the legal registry of children born under this agreement, which affects their right to an identity”.

But while some feminist groups in Mexico have called for the prohibition of surrogacy, the issue remains under debate, with many also feeling that greater regulation is the way forward.

“Far from eradicating the practice, prohibition tends to push it underground, increasing the risks of abuse,” said Esparza.

Oriana López Uribe, co-director of feminist organisation Hilar Talentos, said that, as with sex work, women should be allowed to choose what they want to do with their own bodies.

“The conditions of inequality in which we live aren’t going to change just because a practice is prohibited,” she said. “On the contrary, we are reducing the possibilities that [women] have of obtaining an income.”

And while many argue exploitation is widespread in Mexico, others insist not all surrogacies are exploitative.

Amaro says he and his husband were aware of “the horrible things that happen to surrogates” in Mexico, but once they started talking to other parents who had used the same clinic as them, and who had had “delightful experiences” with their surrogates, their fears were assuaged.

“It was something that worried us a little bit in the beginning but very quickly it became much less relevant,” he said.

The clinic gave them a catalogue “with different profiles of egg donors, with different phenotypes primarily from Latin America”. They chose a young woman from Colombia who the couple felt resembled them physically.

They met their surrogate when they went to sign the surrogacy agreement before a notary, and kept in touch throughout the pregnancy. When their daughter, Gisele, was born, Loup was in the delivery room and both men spent the night in the maternity ward.

After two months in Mexico, the couple returned to France, but are still in contact with the surrogate.

“I send her pictures of Gisele whenever I send pictures to my grandmother every week or two,” Amaro said. “She’s a great person, and we’re really in touch.”

Give it up for Vozinha, Spence and the 2026 World Cup’s cult heroes

The Guardian Sun, 19 Jul 2026 13:19:30 GMT

Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now!

Every World Cup produces cult heroes, icons who make it possible for us to sit back and start misty-eyed recollections by saying: “Do you remember Roger Milla/Saeed Al-Owairan/Keisuke Honda/Paul the Octopus?” Well, the Geopolitics World Cup has not let us down! Here are 10 cult heroes who’ve emerged from this tournament.

Yaya Sithole: a catastrophic start as the South Africa midfielder’s error led to the first goal of the GWC against Mexico, compounded by a second-half red card. Bounced back with a vital display in the win over South Korea, leading his country to the knockout round. Decades from now, people will still be talking about the Yaya Sithole redemption arc. Possibly.

Vozinha: who else? Cape Verde’s players all became cult heroes, but especially the 40-year-old keeper who spent last season in the Portuguese second tier and this summer keeping out Spain as the Blue Sharks went unbeaten in the group stage, then pushed Argentina to extra time in the last 32. Vozinha’s mum: get in line – we’re all in his fan club now.

Djed Spence: a toss-up with Dan “the modern-day header-beast” Burn for England’s cult hero, but let’s give it to the Spurs full-back who transformed from the hapless scourge of Thomas Tuchel’s existence in the group stage to a chin-strapped Cafu in the knockout round. Spence’s slide tackle on Giuliano Simeone (albeit sans chin-strap) will live long in the memory.

Matías Galarza: Paraguay’s most magnificent git was always involved despite rarely trying to play football. Almost every time we saw the midfielder he was moaning, playacting, needling opponents – truly putting the “art” into the dark arts. Also scored against Turkey and later nicked the referee’s watch and strapped it to his own wrist. Timeless ’housery.

Keyne: poor Lamine Yamal, who turned a craggy 19 during the GWC, must be feeling pretty aged considering he’s been usurped by his three-year-old brother. Keyne gurning and giggling in the crowd has delighted fans in Spain and beyond. Considering some of the other people who’ve hogged TV cutaways, the toddler has been a welcome sight.

Iván Barton: Salvadorian referee grabbed the globe’s attention when he sent off Miguel Almirón, bawling at the winger like a mum sending a misbehaving youngster to bed with no dinner. “After review, No 10, Paraguay, covered his mouth! The decision is red card!” No PlayStation either, Miguel!

Eloy Room: move over, Vozinha, and make room for Eloy! Yep, another veteran goalie starred at this GWC as Curaçao bounced back from shipping seven (7) against Germany to hold Ecuador to a 0-0 draw. The 37-year-old Room made 15 saves – a record for a 90-minute World Cup match – to earn the tiny Caribbean island their first ever point.

Danny Murphy: or should it be Bob the cat? The deadpan BBC pundit’s tale of how a family moggy once made a break for freedom inside a Royal Mail van – sparked by Oscar Bobb coming off the bench for Norway – proved so engrossing that viewers demanded, and got, several follow-ups. A purr-fect hydration-break diversion. Honk!

Hossam Hassan: Egypt’s perma-angry, black T-shirted head coach was an intimidating presence – especially paired with his identical twin brother, the team director, Ibrahim Hassan. The pair had a row with Dallas police, led the Pharaohs to the last 16, saw Egypt take a 2-0 lead against Argentina … before the final 15 minutes helped Hossam reach new heights of apoplexy.

Romelu Lukaku: how can Belgium’s record goalscorer be obscure enough for cult-hero status? Well, when you polish off USA USA USA 4-1 and celebrate your 93rd international goal with a Trump dance near the corner flag in the aftermath of Balogungate. Thanks, Big Rom (Bigliest Rom?) – the planet is with you.

Join Rob Smyth from 8pm BST (3pm EST, 5am AEST) for hot updates from Spain 1-1 Argentina (aet; 4-5 on pens) in the GWC final. The animals below agree, though the punters in New York City disagree. Meanwhile Tom Lutz will be in situ for another liveblog mopping up all other business outside the game, which we’re tempted to call Everything But The Goal.

“This game will help us for sure – even if you can never fully celebrate a bronze medal. It’s the first [men’s World Cup] medal for 60 years, first [at a men’s] World Cup on foreign soil, and I hope the players can be proud of that at some point. We set ourselves the highest dream to chase, and we were very, very ambitious with our dream to make the final in the World Cup. So it’s very, very painful if you miss out, the pain will stay for a while” – England head coach Thomas Tuchel after overseeing a quite preposterous 6-4 win over France in the Third Place Play-off.

When Maga’s power fades, we cannot abandon those ICE killed

The Guardian Sun, 19 Jul 2026 13:00:28 GMT

When this is all over, people will tell us to move on. But those who perpetrated this reign of terror must be held accountable

One day, when Maga is out of power and the conditions of political possibility have changed, there are going to be people who tell you that the best thing for the country is to move on. There are going to be people who tell you that attempts to hold the purveyors of Trumpism accountable are petty, vindictive, engaging in a kind of petulant recrimination and score-settling. There are going to be people who tell you that there must not be investigations, that it would be a waste of time to have trials. There are going to be people who tell you that it is not wise to change the law to allow for prosecutions and lawsuits; that too great an emphasis on the past will only divide the country, and keep us from looking toward the future. This argument was made after Watergate; it was made after the civil war. It was wrong back then, and it will be wrong again when it is delivered, with piety and smugness, after Trump.

When Maga leaves power, all of the officers, bureaucrats and leaders of ICE – from the uniformed thugs in masks on the streets, to the contractors guarding concentration camps, to the suited vultures directing the operation in Washington and drafting legal memos to justify it – all of them must be held accountable. Their immunity from criminal prosecution and civil suits must be eradicated, and their liability must be made retroactive. They must be investigated, tried, fined, punished and ostracized. Needless to say, ICE must be abolished – attempts to merely reform it must be resisted as betrayals of democratic values. But it is not enough to abolish ICE. Those who are responsible for ICE must be driven from public life.

This much is clear from a slew of recent deaths. Last Tuesday, a business owner and father of three named Lorenzo Salgado Araujo was shot dead in his car by an ICE agent in Houston while he was on his way to work. At 52, he had made an honorable and prosperous life for himself in Texas after immigrating from Mexico 35 years ago, at age 17. His three co-workers who were in the car – he had picked them up to give them a ride to work – survived the shooting, and were disappeared into ICE custody. Later, it turned out that the ICE agents had been looking for somebody else.

Before Salgado’s body was even cold, ICE killed again. Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero was a 25-year-old resident of Biddeford, Maine, who had been born in Colombia. According to his father, he had a work permit, a condition typical of asylum claimants. He worked two jobs – one as a food delivery driver, and another as a custodian at a veterinary office – to support his wife and three-year-old daughter. According to witnesses, his little girl witnessed the ICE agents ram into her father’s car, approach his driver’s side window and then shoot her father dead. The incident occurred at about 7am; the little girl was still in her Bluey pajamas. Angus King, a senator from Maine, was told by the DHS secretary, Markwayne Mullen, that ICE was looking for somebody else when they killed Durán, too.

After the agents killed him, ICE proclaimed that Salgado had been trying to run them down with his car, a statement that witnesses have contested. It’s also exactly what ICE said about Renee Good, the mother of three they killed in Minneapolis early this year. Video quickly disproved ICE’s account of the Good killing; there is no reason to think that their account of Salgado’s death is true, either.

What seems more likely: ICE, a group of reckless, trigger-happy bigots tasked with carrying out the president’s mass deportation and ethnic cleansing regime, is terrorizing communities, stalking disfavored populations, targeting innocent, hardworking people on the basis of their race, and often escalating their interactions to deadly violence.

We have been here before. The needless, cold-blooded shootings of Salgado and Durán come months after ICE killed two US citizens in Minneapolis, first Good and then the Veterans Affairs hospital nurse Alex Pretti. Their deaths galvanized an already robust civilian anti-ICE resistance in Minneapolis, and sparked protests across the country against ICE’s kidnapping and ethnic cleansing operations. The bad PR clearly got to the president; Greg Bovino, the high-profile border patrol commander who became famous for his Nazi-like attire, lost his job, apparently as a concession to the unpopularity of the raids; Kristi Noem, the Homeland Security secretary who ran the department at the time, didn’t last long, either. But after a brief de-escalation, ICE has now resumed its raids with their former ostentatious cruelty, needless violence and terrorizing gore. “ICE hunts us like animals,” Maria Cervantes, a Mexican immigrant who lives in the Houston neighborhood where ICE killed Salgado, told the Guardian. “I can’t help but think, who’s next? Am I going to get a bullet to the head for being brown?”

If we are to rebuild America as a new kind of country – if we are to make it fulfill its promise to be a free and pluralistic democracy of equals – then we have an obligation to make sure that no one ever has to ask that question again, and that those who do receive justice for the suffering, violence and indignity that this regime has inflicted on them. When this is all over, people will tell you to move on. What they will not tell you is that moving on requires forgetting about Salgado, and Durán, and about Good and Pretti, and about everyone else that ICE has killed and will kill. It will require you to leave the insult and injustice of their deaths unanswered. We must refuse to.

Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnist

Going offline is fun. Living offline was not – just ask a child of the 90s

The Guardian Sun, 19 Jul 2026 13:00:27 GMT

The neo-luddites are fighting the good fight. But my life before smartphones felt lonelier and more dangerous

Welcome to the Summer of Ludd. That’s the name of an anti-smartphone festival recently held in New York. It was slightly under the radar for obvious reasons – there was no Instagram, TikTok or website; advertisements were on “wheatpasted monochrome posters”. Those attending followed the rules: “Be present, and absolutely no phones, recording, or photos allowed.”

That’s perhaps why, the Economist reported, “crowds were small” – but they seemed to be having fun, with events including “Google in Real Life” (festival attenders answering questions on their specialist subjects), “flirting rehabilitation” and “hanging out with rats”. I was particularly charmed by the festival’s “media spokespuppet”, Gowanus: more events should be fronted by carpet offcuts with sock arms and button eyes.

A wider neo-luddite movement is gathering momentum. You may have read about gen Z prioritising IRL socialising, “going 90s” and adopting offline, old-fashioned hobbies. The likes of Offline Club and New York University’s IRL initiative are combating smartphone addiction with phone-free spaces and events.

There’s a gentle longing for analogue fun – reading big books, dreaming, making things, being silly. I see it in my gen Z sons: they have paper diaries, CDs and old-school hobbies (playing instruments, embroidery). And they’re much more disciplined about screen time than their parents: one brought his Brick (a device you tap with your phone, blocking access to time-sucking apps) on holiday.

It’s combined with a strong strand of starker techno-pessimism that warns we’re teetering on the brink of AI-engineered oblivion; that smartphones and social media are tools of oppression and surveillance, and tech companies are engaged in “systematic fracking of human beings”, extracting our attention for profit. Hopefully, they’re wrong about the imminent extinction bit, but it’s increasingly evident they’re right about the rest.

So is this the summer we copy the original luddites with automated looms and grind our smartphones to piles of glass shards, copper and lithium? Realising how much of my life is dominated by my phone makes me itch to hang out with rats and dance with Gowanus.

But hang on: I was there before phones, and some of it was absolutely crap – the friction for which friction-maxxers yearn was abundantly, luxuriantly available. If we’re heading back in that direction – and I accept we should – let’s go clear-eyed.

For a start, it was dangerous. Driving anywhere new meant navigating with a giant, floppy map book precariously propped on the dashboard and scribbled handwritten directions on the passenger seat. I’m an awful driver at the best of times, and flailing around with paper at every motorway exit and junction placed me and other road users in constant peril. Another example: when I was working in Normandy in 1995, getting home from an inexplicably popular nightclub located in a field meant riding in a dilapidated banger driven by someone who had been drinking for six hours straight. In both cases – and so many more – I survived thanks to luck alone.

It was also lonely. If you were awkward or socially inept, if your life was restricted by illness, caring responsibilities or geography, if you just never quite found your people, life could feel awfully empty and isolated. I spent years lacking connection (the nightclub trips were a rare exception, and I didn’t actually enjoy them) and thinking I was unlikable – maybe I was! But my life blossomed in the “blogosphere” and on Twitter (as it then was); it was improved and enriched beyond recognition by people I met online.

And God, it was sometimes so boring. That student who said she would “stare at a wall” when the under-16 social media ban came in was accurately describing most of my adolescence. I think you might be less inclined to say “boredom is good for you” if you’d spent every Saturday night for years watching Casualty with your mum (no shade, she was great company, but Charlie Fairhead wasn’t). The tech-shunners may well find that a Summer of Ludd is an easier sell than a winter, when it’s rainy, cold and dark before 4pm.

I still think the neo-luddites are right and fighting the good fight. But switching off will be hard. Maybe hardest for my generation – the people who lived the before-and-after-smartphones eras most vividly, feeling the world open up in wild, digital Technicolor in the palms of our hands.

Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnist

The truth about migraines: what causes them – and how to find relief

The Guardian Sun, 19 Jul 2026 13:00:27 GMT

Over the last decade, the understanding of these devastating headaches has grown enormously, as has the understanding of what can be done to treat them

We’ve been trying to cure migraines – without much success, until relatively recently – for as long as we’ve been able to identify them as a distinct ailment. The Ebers Papyrus, a scroll dating back to 1550BC that mentions a “disease of one half of the head”, suggests anointing the scalp with fried catfish; Galen, the second-century Roman physician whose term “hemicrania” evolved into the modern word, recommended blood-letting (this, to be fair, was his answer to a lot of things). By the 20th century, doctors were suggesting repressed emotions might be at fault, leading to suggestions that women – who suffer from migraines far more than men – were simply too fragile and neurotic. As recently as a couple of decades ago, “vascular theory” – the idea that blood vessels in the brain expanding and contracting were to blame – was still the standard explanation in many medical schools.

Over the last decade, though, our understanding of what causes these neurological disorders, which are technically a sub-category of headache, has progressed enormously, alongside the options for treating them. One of the biggest problems, as in centuries past, is a lack of sympathy for sufferers. The biggest difference, these days, is that we actually understand what is happening, and why.

Before we get into the brain science, it’s helpful to understand that headaches, more generally, fit into two broad categories: primary headaches, which don’t come from any underlying structural cause, and secondary headaches, which could be caused by anything from stroke, meningitis or a tumour, to bleeding on the brain. A hangover, which is caused by a number of factors (some of them related to dehydration), is secondary – but a cluster headache, a very unpleasant neurological condition that can be triggered by alcohol in a matter of minutes, is primary. Migraines are primary, but are frequently mistaken for secondary: one of the many reasons that sufferers have often been poorly served.

“As doctors, we’re taught to ask the right questions to determine which type of headache it is,” says Alexandra Sinclair, a professor of neurology at the University of Birmingham and chair of the British Association for the Study of Headache. “We use the International Headache Society classification, which you can see online – but actually, for the individual patient, many headaches feel quite similar, so the precise classification can be difficult to understand. Generally, though, a headache that is moderate to severe, where a patient wants to lie down, keep away from light, and noise, keep still, may feel nauseated, and feels pounding pain, often on one side – that’s most often going to be migraine.”

Migraines, we now understand, come from the activation of the trigeminovascular system – a network of nerves and blood vessels that detects pain in the brain. The core of this system is the largest and most complex sensory nerve in your head: the trigeminal nerve, which deals with sensory information (including touch, pain, temperature) and motor control (chewing). When something goes wrong, the nerve fibres in this system pump out a chemical called CGRP (calcitonin gene-related peptide), which activates the brain’s pain network and causes headaches that range from moderate to crippling.

Something else that’s now better understood is that migraines typically occur over four phases, including a warning period that might include excess yawning, urination or fatigue. A common occurrence at this stage is odd food cravings – which can lead to an element of victim-blaming. “Historically, there used to be a sense of ‘Well, you may have caused your headache by eating a piece of cheese or chocolate,’” says Prof Sinclair. “But actually, the research has completely turned that upside down. Functional brain imaging shows activation of the brain areas that might make you crave food in the 24 hours or so before the actual pain. Hence, you didn’t cause the migraine – the migraine caused the craving.”

After this period – technically called the “prodrome” – about 30% of sufferers experience what is known as the “aura”, which can include visual disturbances, numbness in the face or arms or legs, or speech difficulties. Then there’s the migraine itself, which typically lasts anywhere from four to 72 hours. Then finally the “postdrome”, where you may feel washed out or exhausted for up to two days. It’s typically only after that, after several days of disruption to your body’s typical way of functioning, that things go back to normal.

Like other systems in the body, this network of sensations probably evolved for good reasons. “There are schools of thought that would say that when you get meningitis or when you have a head injury or something going on in your brain like a tumor, you may be primed to get more headaches, which actually may be good – because it alerts you that something’s happened within your brain,” says Prof Sinclair. “There are also schools of thought that say that back in our caveman days, if you were primed to have migraines, you’d be quite vigilant, to noise, light, or movement – you probably wouldn’t be sleeping deeply – and so those genes might have stayed with us by giving humans a survival advantage.”

This, in a nutshell, is the issue for severe migraine sufferers. Hormonal, lifestyle and even environmental changes can change your susceptibility to what is technically a neurological disease, but you can also have a brain that’s genetically primed to be more headache-prone. These days, of course, more of us are working in fluorescent-lit offices than keeping watch around a campfire – and if a migraine hobbles our ability to get any work done for most of the week, then it’s no longer a survival advantage (the World Health Organization, for instance, lists migraine in the top 10 “most disabling” diseases globally).

“It affects a huge number of people for what should be the most productive years of their lives, frequently between puberty and menopause,” says Prof Sinclair. “For some people, their ability to function properly is impaired for much of the month – and then there’s the stigma around it not being a ‘real’ issue, and being sort of pushed to the back of the queue for medical treatment.” About twice as many women seem to suffer from migraine as men, for reasons that run from hormonal differences to differences in brain susceptibility to pain chemicals. That might be another reason it traditionally hasn’t been treated seriously enough.

There are things sufferers can do to mitigate the likelihood of migraine: lack of sleep, too much sleep, caffeine withdrawal, dehydration and significant stress all play a part. Screen time, according to the available evidence, presents a murkier picture: migraine sufferers are typically sensitive to light, but it’s not totally established that there’s a correlation between phone or monitor use and the onset of attacks.

The good news? The identification of CGRP means that migraine treatments are now improving rapidly, consisting of inhibitors built specifically to block the pain chemical. “We have a class of drugs usually taken as a tablet called Gepants that work by blocking the CGRP receptor,” says Prof Sinclair. “We also have CGRP monoclonal antibodies, often referred to as Mabs, which are typically administered via monthly injection. Together, they have truly revolutionised headache care over the last four or five years.” The problem is, these treatments are expensive, and can be difficult to access. “We need more healthcare professionals able to provide headache management, alongside a simpler prescribing process, so patients can access treatment when they need it and recover faster,” says Prof Sinclair. “But we also need to educate patients to seek help. Effective management is essential and can sometimes be the difference between losing your job or keeping it. So I think it’s really about understanding that, if you’re a migraine sufferer, things really have changed.”

Headaches might not have altered in 2,000 years, but thankfully we’ve moved past seeing them as a badge of character.

Nigel Farage admits George Cottrell paid for filming and let him use his home

The Guardian Sun, 19 Jul 2026 12:21:32 GMT

Reform leader says support from fraudster before last election is ‘totally undeclarable in every single way’

Nigel Farage has admitted his close friend the fraudster George Cottrell let him use one of his London homes and paid for social media filming before the last election but insisted it was “totally undeclarable in every single way”.

The Reform UK leader spoke in depth for the first time about his support from Cottrell and the £5m gift from the Thailand-based businessman Christopher Harborne in an interview with the anti-woke Triggernometry podcast.

He acknowledged the parliamentary standards system could find against him but claimed he had sought advice from a “top international lawyer” who told him the £5m did not need to be declared because it was unconditional.

In relation to Cottrell, Farage said his friend had given him nothing since he was elected in July 2024 and that financial support before then was “irrelevant” and unrelated to politics.

The Reform UK leader also claimed his party was being unfairly targeted over a £500,000 donation to the party from Cottrell’s mother, Fiona, which is under investigation by the police over whether she is the true source of the funding.

However, in an apparent slip of the tongue, Farage referred to it as being a donation from Cottrell himself, before correcting himself to say it was from his mother, as he made the case that it was a conspiracy against the party.

“The idea that his donation – it was his mother’s donation – this was reported to the NCA [National Crime Agency] in September 2024. The police followed up in the spring of 2025. Why is it now a story? It’s now a story because everything is being coordinated together to try and knock us out of the game. That’s why I’m fighting this byelection. I’m saying: let the people decide.”

Farage’s support in kind from Cottrell and the £5m from Harborne just before the last election are currently under investigation by the standards commissioner over whether they should have been publicly registered.

Financial support has to be declared within 12 months of an MP being elected if it has any link to their political activities.

Although the standards commissioner has not yet reported back, Farage has called a byelection in his constituency of Clacton to let voters decide if they want him as MP, although it is being boycotted by the major parties. He could face a second byelection if the commissioner finds against him and the penalty is enough to trigger a recall petition.

On the financial support he took from Cottrell before July 2024, Farage told the podcast: “At that period of my life, from 2021 to 3 June 2024, I was a broadcaster, I was someone that appeared on celebrity TV programmes, I was somebody that promoted some financial market products, I was an influencer, I had a considerable 5 million following, so the fact that George did me a favour with those things is not a matter of public interest or record. It’s irrelevant. I wasn’t in politics, it’s literally no one’s business and it is totally undeclarable in every single way.”

He also defended his decision to stay loyal to Cottrell, who is a member of his inner circle and who Farage described as an “enormously colourful character”.

On Cottrell’s conviction and imprisonment for fraud in the US in 2017, Farage said: “George, as a young man, got into trouble in America. If you are involved in tax avoidance schemes, it is very easy in America to get into very, very big trouble.”

Reform UK is also under scrutiny over £1m sent by Fiona Cottrell before the last election to Britain Means Business, a company controlled by the Reform UK deputy leader, Richard Tice. Of this, £500,000 was later sent to Reform UK by Britain Means Business.

The Guardian has previously reported that Fiona Cottrell did not send the money straight to the Britain Means Business account. It was routed via a UK bank account of an Australian money exchange platform called Oneify.

The Sunday Times reported this weekend that George Cottrell opened an account with a money transfer firm called Oneify in May 2024.

Asked this month if Cottrell transferred money to his mother before she made donations to Reform, his lawyers at Carter-Ruck said: “Our client has confirmed his instructions that any donations by his mother have been entirely her own decision.” The lawyers added: “He therefore declines to engage with your [wider] questions.”

In a previous letter to the Guardian, the lawyers stated that “his mother’s donations have been entirely her own decision, and are a matter for her”. They added that suggestions he “has donated impermissibly to Reform UK are unfounded”. Fiona Cottrell has declined to speak to the media about the donations.

Corded vacuums are supposed to be outdated – so why is the Shark Detect Lift-Away XL so good?

The Guardian Sun, 19 Jul 2026 12:00:26 GMT

Surprisingly easy to manoeuvre and skilled at cleaning carpet and hard floor, Shark’s upright bagless model is one of the best corded vacuums I’ve tested

The best vacuum cleaners

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Corded vacuum cleaners aren’t as glamorous as their cordless cousins, but swapping battery power for a plug socket has its advantages. The device will never be short of power, so it can keep cleaning for as long as you need it to. Prices also tend to be lower because there’s no expensive battery to factor into the cost.

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

On the downside, there’s a cable to manage while you clean, and even the longest cords usually need to be switched from one plug socket to another if your home is any larger than a small flat.

The Shark Detect XL LA791UKT is a versatile corded upright that carries many of the best elements you’ll find on Shark’s cordless vacuums. Chief among these is the Duo Clean dual-roller floor head, which combines a fluffy roller and a regular brush bar into an all-in-one unit. That makes it an expert on carpets and hard floors, without needing to switch heads.

What’s relatively new to this model is its Detect function. This is a sensor on the underside of the floor head that works out what surface it’s on and adjusts the speed of its rollers accordingly. That means you don’t have to flip a switch when transferring from the hard floor of your kitchen or utility room to carpets and rugs in your living areas.

Corded vacuum cleaners aren’t as difficult to test as cordless models, as there’s no battery life to take into consideration. I tested the suction by attaching a gauge to the end of the extension hose and recording the measurements on minimum and maximum modes.

I also put the vacuum through a series of cleaning tests, challenging it to collect pre-weighed amounts of cat litter, flour and pet hair using the Duo Clean floor head. I ran these tests on short-pile carpet and hard floor, weighing the collection bin before and after each test to find out how much mess is transferred from the floor to the bin.

There’s little here that’s particularly new or exciting, but frankly, that’s the way I like Shark’s vacuum cleaners. They’ve been blitzing my cleaning tests for several generations now, and change isn’t always for the better, as we saw with the Dyson V16 Piston Animal.

The Duo Clean floor head is a refined and effective piece of engineering that Shark is sensibly tweaking without revolutionising. The surface detection is the newest addition to the corded range, but many of Shark’s cordless vacuums (such as our favourite, the Shark PowerDetect Clean & Empty IP3251) already have that feature. The classic two rollers and anti-tangle system are unchanged from previous models, and rightly so – it carries on a fine tradition here, performing well in my tests.

The collection bin can be released from the floor head by pressing a foot pedal, then lifted away. You can then release the handle from the extension wand to use it as a handheld device (albeit on the end of the flexible hose). And the bin is a good size, with a capacity of 2.5 litres. That isn’t as voluminous as some corded devices, with a regular-size bagged Henry typically swallowing six litres of dirt before it needs emptying, but it’s still more than twice the capacity of most cordless vacuum cleaners.

As a result, it’s large and heavy to lug around, weighing 5.2kg on my bathroom scales. Leave the floor head behind in Lift-Away mode, however, and it drops to a more manageable 2.9kg, including the 8m cable, handle and extension.

Despite its weight, it’s surprisingly nimble when it’s on the floor and switched on. Its centre of gravity is low, and the floor head pulls forwards slightly on carpet. If anything, you need to rein in its enthusiasm, rather than struggle to get it moving.

Weight: 5.2kgMax suction power (quoted): not statedMax suction power (measured): 17kPaCord length: 8mDust capacity: 2.5lAdditional filters supplied? NoDimensions: 31 x 43 x 115cm (WDH)

With the combination of the floor head and an excellent variety of attachments, the thing I love most about this vacuum cleaner is its ability to clean up every mess thrown at it. I was particularly impressed with the floor head’s performance in my flour and pet hair tests. On carpets and hard floors, the vacuum easily lifted everything I spilt.

The cat litter proved marginally more elusive, with a small number of pieces falling out of the vacuum when I finished cleaning, having not made it into the collection bin. It’s beside the point, though, because I managed to clean up the remainder quickly and easily using the extension wand without any attachments. The cat litter flew up the tube, a better way to gather larger particles than forcing them through the floor head.

And the attachments really are excellent, including the ones I always look for: a motorised upholstery tool, and a combination crevice tool and dusting brush. I tested the floor head’s anti-tangle capability on my daughter’s bedroom floor. This has proved to be a tricky test for many rival vacuum cleaners because of her long hair, which is highly prone to wrapping itself around a vacuum’s rollers. Shark’s system has a comb that lifts out the hair before it gets tangled – and it performed its job perfectly here. I could see hair coming off the floor and saw it pass safely into the collection bin. I inspected the rollers closely afterwards, and couldn’t see a single strand left behind.

It’s great to be able to lift the collection bin away from the floor head when you want to access hard-to-reach areas, whether they’re high up, such as cobwebs in the corners, or you’re cleaning the stairs. This makes it a bit lighter, less bulky, and leaves the wheels behind. I found the motorised upholstery tool particularly effective for the stairs, though I did need to follow it up with the crevice tool to tackle the edges and corners. With the main vacuum section in one hand and the released handle and hose in the other, accessing difficult areas is a breeze.

Sign up to The Filter

Get the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.

after newsletter promotion

The controls are incredibly simple, with no screen or menus to navigate. The vacuum is switched on via a button on the main unit. This doubles up as a mode switch, which can either be left in Detect mode or forced to stay in either carpet or hard-floor modes. The only downside is that you have to reach down to the collection bin to operate it, whereas many cordless vacuums have their controls more readily available at the handle.

It’s also possible to control the suction power with a flick of a switch. This is up at the handle, so it can be controlled with a thumb while you’re vacuuming. There are two modes, Min and Max, with the Min setting essentially opening up a vent that lets through more air, thus weakening the suction.

Cordless vacuum cleaners are reasonably good at getting under low furniture, but the Shark’s floor head is held back by the bulk of the collection bin that sits above it. You can certainly use one of the attachments to reach difficult places, but you don’t quite get the flexibility and manoeuvrability of a cordless here.

I also didn’t love the cord. While eliminating the chance of running out of power, cord management while you’re vacuuming is an extra thing to think about. The Shark doesn’t have fancy retractable cord storage either – instead you’re required to wrap the cord around two hooks on the side when you’ve finished your cleaning.

I’ve used a few similar upright Sharks extensively for everyday cleaning jobs and found that they can suffer blockages due to the slightly convoluted path that debris has to pass through. Even when the floor head is attached, dirt is sucked up the extension wand, almost up to the handle, then back down the bendy tube to the collection bin. I didn’t experience any blockages during testing, but have witnessed it in similar designs. Fortunately, everything is easy to dismantle, so blockages are simple to clear. They also only really occur when you’re tackling particularly problematic messes, such as clumps of pet hair.

Shark’s corded vacuum cleaners have a generous five-year guarantee, provided you register the product within 28 days of purchase. The guarantee covers parts and labour, and Shark offers repair or replacement if things go wrong with your machine. It doesn’t cover blockages, misuse or everyday wear and tear – such as worn-out rollers or blown fuses – but most other types of fault are covered.

Although it doesn’t use bags, the LA791UKT does have a consumable in the form of an anti-odour capsule. These aren’t essential to replace, but they keep your vacuum smelling a little more pleasant, and last for about six months. Shark sells replacement cartridges for £7.99 each.

The filters are easy to remove and wash under cold running water. There are two pre-motor filters, which should be rinsed through and left to dry once a month. The post-motor filter is an annual cleaning job. If any of these get too bunged up, you can buy replacements from Shark.

When your vacuum finally gives up, it can be recycled at a local electrical recycling centre – find your nearest at recycle-more.

For more, read our guide on how to make your vacuum cleaner last longer

The Shark Detect Lift-Away XL LA791UKT is easily the best corded vacuum cleaner I’ve tested, with excellent performance in my tests, all the add-ons and attachments you could ask for, and no-fuss operation and maintenance. At an RRP of £349.99, it’s at the higher end of Shark’s price scale for corded upright vacuum cleaners, but it comes with everything you might need and a guarantee that should ensure it’s built to last.

His greatest weakness is that he never, ever remembers how things came out of their packaging, so they rarely fit back in again when it’s time to return them

Trump’s rebranding of Palm Beach airport hasn’t taken off as he planned

The Guardian Sun, 19 Jul 2026 12:00:26 GMT

Changes inside the Florida international airport are hardly evident as state and county hold back funds for full remodel

One of Donald Trump’s most grandiose vanity projects, a multimillion-dollar makeover of Florida’s Palm Beach international airport into a self-aggrandizing, gold-plated transportation hub, is running into turbulence, barely a week after the first plane’s wheels touched the runway.

At first glance, the rebranding of the airport less than 5 miles from his opulent Mar-a-Lago resort appears to be complete. Its website bears the name and oversized logo of the President Donald J Trump international airport, and state transportation workers were quick to erect highway signs leaving drivers in no doubt where they were heading.

Yet inside the terminals, at the ticket counters and baggage halls, the change is far less noticeable. Digital signage reflects the switch, but many physical signs and infrastructure still refer to its old name of Palm Beach International (PBI).

There is no clear timeline of when, or even if, new signs will be installed and PBI fully becomes DJT, the three-letter airport code using the president’s initials that will be its formal aviation industry designation starting on 18 August.

The issue is money. A state law signed in March by Ron DeSantis, Florida’s Republican governor and intermittent Trump ally, mandated the name change on a reluctant county commission, which voted 4-3 in May to approve a trademark deal with the Trump Organization as some members feared consequences if they did not.

But Florida’s $117.6bn budget signed off by DeSantis last month contained only $2.75m to fund the switch, half of the estimated $5.5m overall cost. And Palm Beach county is refusing to make up the shortfall, with some commissioners insisting taxpayers cannot and should not be left on the hook.

“We will be able to make the baseline, necessary changes to signage with the $2,750,000. But for the full extensive signage, we will be needing the other half of those funds from the state,” Joseph Abruzzo, the county administrator, told the Miami Herald.

Abruzzo was speaking on 9 July, the official handover day when “Trump Force One” carrying the president’s son Eric landed just after 5am to become the first to do so under the airport’s new name.

A statement on the airport’s website, meanwhile, says that, beyond the $2.75m received in state money: “The remaining costs will be funded through the [Palm Beach county] Department of Airports’ operating budget and capital improvement program.”

It is an apparent contradiction to Abruzzo’s remarks to the media last week that no county money will be used, and has raised fears among some critics that funds earmarked for safety and other crucial improvements at the department’s four airports, which include Palm Beach international, will be siphoned off to support Trump’s glorification.

Joel Flores, one of three county commissioners to vote against the unorthodox trademark and licensing agreement in May that critics say will further enrich the president and his family, said he would attempt to block any such move.

“I will not personally be voting to utilize any operational funds towards this rebranding,” he said.

“This should be solely on the state to be able to fund this. This is their initiative. This is their imposition, their rule over a local municipality over a local airport, so they should be responsible.

“We’ve also heard that, federally, they might be sending some dollars down, but I have not seen any bills or budgets that address that. So until I see the money in the bank, I’m not going to count with it.”

Flores said he agreed with Abruzzo’s assessment that the rebranding would move forward in phases, and stall until more funds were found.

“That’s the kind of conversation I’ve had with our administrator,” he said. “If we don’t get to rebrand entirely, then that’s on them. I don’t feel that our dollars should be going to a rebrand that this board did not approve.”

Rebeca Krogman, the public information officer for the Palm Beach department of airports, said a phased approach “ensures continued progress while aligning each step with available resources”.

In a statement, she said: “As with any facility of this size, it would not be practical to list every individual sign or area that has or has not yet been updated.

“We have begun updating all digital touchpoints, including the airport’s website, social media platforms, and digital signage within the terminal. Temporary signage is also being deployed across the campus pending installation of permanent signage, including the large welcome sign on Turnage Boulevard.”

Krogman did not rule out drawing on the airports’ operating budget, but said it was not the department’s preference.

“It is our intent to continue these improvements through the airport’s normal budgeting process, primarily utilizing available external funding sources, such as the recent state allocation for signage upgrades, while actively pursuing additional opportunities, including legislative appropriations and grant funding,” she said.

The Florida department of transportation did not return a request for comment.

Two lawsuits have also been filed to try to prevent the rebranding from advancing. One is by George Poncy, a retired pilot who said that changing the airport’s identifier from PBI, which has been embedded in air traffic control and aviation navigation and management software for decades, will cause confusion that could create a safety hazard.

The other, by the trademark attorney Victoria Doyle, argues the state had no authority to impose the name change on a county-owned and -operated airport.

Doyle, who is running for the Democratic nomination for a Palm Beach congressional seat in next month’s primary election, said her case has been granted a trial date next year.

“Trump’s ego is going to demand upgrades to that airport as fast as possible,” she said.

“He’s going to want it to be the best, most beautiful, most gold-laden airport on earth, and we could be on the hook. I am suspicious of all statements about funding and wouldn’t be surprised if the county ends up paying the money.

“The airport is an extremely upsetting topic to many people here. We are a majority Democratic county, and we were not asked our opinion of this renaming. It was shoved down our throats from the state on high, and the money is a big part of why they’re so upset. Not only did we not want this rename, now we’re going to have to pay for it? It’s highly offensive to people who live here.”

Are money and soft power draining World Cup football of its magic?

The Guardian Sun, 19 Jul 2026 11:16:50 GMT

Fifa’s orchestration of incompatible or frankly absurd corporate sponsorship suggests the balance may have tipped too far

It’s almost all over. No more hydration breaks, no more obligatory pans of the TV cameras to Hollywood A-listers, or dread of the crushing inevitability of English disappointment. The Fifa World Cup 2026 is at an end, after another month of planet-straddling drama laced with significance and symbolism, both on and off the pitch.

Before the kick-off between Spain and Argentina on Sunday evening, the result is already clear: football’s greatest prize is more than a sporting event; it is a geopolitically charged economic juggernaut.

After a month of fixtures, billions of dollars have been spent in an extravaganza of consumerism and corporate largesse, fuelled by advertising spend, ticket sales, merchandise, gambling, travel and hospitality. Fifa estimates that the tournament will add $40.9bn (£30.4bn) to global GDP, with the US – ahead of Canada and Mexico as the leading economy among the co-host nations – accounting for almost half of the total.

There are good reasons for the World Cup’s economic impact: no other sporting event – not even the Olympics, Tour de France or Wimbledon – can match its global reach. Sunday’s final is expected to draw an audience at least 10 times that of the Super Bowl.

According to Fifa, more than half the world’s population – about 5 billion people – were estimated to have watched at least part of the last World Cup in Qatar in 2022. With the competition’s expanded format this year, total engagement is expected to be higher still.

Big sporting and cultural events can be significant money-spinners able to send ripples through the wider economy. Taylor Swift’s 2024 Eras tour supposedly pushed up quarterly GDP in Britain and Singapore, and a Beyoncé concert was blamed for driving up inflation in Sweden.

But the impact is not always entirely clear-cut. Using data from the 1982 World Cup onwards, analysts at Goldman Sachs found only a marginally positive effect on economic output for the host nation. The long-run effects are also virtually zero: while activity is boosted short term, much of the spending is often simply redirected from other activities, and any boom during the finals is often followed by a decline afterwards.

Early analysis by the US Federal Reserve shows that, while some bars in Boston ran out of booze as Scotland fans descended on the city, the positive impact was mitigated by economic weakness elsewhere as consumers cut back amid rising prices linked to the Iran war. Regular tourists have also avoided host cities because of anticipated congestion and sky-high prices.

There are intangible benefits, however. Goldman’s analysts point out that many fans would pay over the odds to see their country win. The sense of national pride, happiness and cultural heft is large, and difficult to quantify on the cold-hearted GDP ledger.

Riding on the coat-tails of the World Cup is also, clearly, big business. The corporate sponsors have cashed in, with airlines, bars, restaurants, hotels and retailers across the 48 nations involved also ringing in profits. But this is about more than just money: it is about soft power and who wields it.

Just look at Fifa’s official sponsors. Each shines a spotlight: Qatar Airways and Saudi Aramco, among the top-tier “partners” – believed to be paying up to $200m for the privilege – underline the dominance of fossil fuels in powering global output, and the influence seeking of the energy-rich Gulf states. Adidas, Coca-Cola and Visa cling on for the old guard of western capitalism, while the fast-growing economies of Asia are represented by the South Korean carmaker Hyundai-Kia and the Chinese technology company Lenovo.

Below them, the cadre of “sponsors” and commercial “supporters” range from a crypto exchange to tech companies, banks, and even an “official dairy sponsor” in China’s Mengniu Dairy. Not all sound that compatible with elite sport – not least the “quick-service restaurant sponsor” McDonald’s, or official snack food sponsor Frito-Lay (known better in the UK as Walkers). Some border on the absurd: does the World Cup need a bespoke Louis Vuitton trophy trunk to be carried on to the pitch in New York? Even the clothes worn by Fifa’s officials are a money-spinning opportunity, for “official formal wear supplier” Boggi Milano, an Italian fashion house.

Sign up to Business Today

after newsletter promotion

Sixty years ago, when England lifted the trophy in 1966, pitch-side advertising – for brands including Brylcreem and Gordon’s Gin – crept into the tournament for the first time. A year earlier, the Rolling Stones lambasted the dawn of the modern consumerist age (“He can’t be a man ‘cause he doesn’t smoke the same cigarettes as me”). Today? The band has a “landmark collaboration” with world football’s governing body to sell three limited-edition vinyl album covers, and a remixed song for the Official Fifa World Cup 2026™ Album.

As the ringmaster, Fifa is expected to earn a small fortune – with projections it will rake in more than the $7.6bn it earned at the 2022 Qatar World Cup.

Part of the reason for the commercial whirl is understandable. Fifa’s mission is to grow and develop football in each of its 211 member associations – from the grassroots to elite competition; youth, women’s football and education programmes. It is laudable stuff. For all of the rivalry in football, the game still brings people together – despite our fragmenting world.

It would also be foolish to pretend that money and power have no place in the beautiful game. The kicking of a pig’s bladder in medieval Britain would not have developed into a global sport without the spread of empire. Money has also long played an outsize role in the business of winning trophies, in a relationship that, although riven with tension, is ultimately symbiotic.

But has the balance tipped too far? Such corporate encroachment, into a game with deep working-class roots, is increasingly fraught in an age when globalisation is being questioned and the fruits of trickle-down economics have turned sour.
